Tech Report: Introducing RTEB: A Latest Standard for Retrieval Evaluation

📅 01 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1018 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a upcoming benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications.
  • In a recent development, the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval.
  • It has been revealed that this is where things get tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that TL;DR – We’re excited to introduce the beta version of the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB), a upcoming benchmark designed to reliably evaluate the retrieval accuracy of embedding models for real-world applications. Existing benchmarks struggle to measure true generalization, while RTEB addresses this with a hybrid strategy of open and private datasets. Its goal is simple: to create a fair, transparent, and application-focused standard for measuring how models perform on data they haven’t seen before.

In a recent development, the performance of many AI applications, from RAG and agents to recommendation systems, is fundamentally limited by the quality of search and retrieval. As such, accurately measuring the retrieval quality of embedding models is a common pain point for developers. How do you really know how well a model will perform in the wild?

It has been revealed that this is where things get tricky. The current standard for evaluation often relies on a model's "zero-shot" performance on public benchmarks. However, this is, at best, an approximation of a model's true generalization capabilities. When models are repeatedly evaluated against the same public datasets, a gap emerges between their reported scores and their actual performance on new, unseen data.

To address these challenges, we developed RTEB, a benchmark built to provide a reliable standard for evaluating retrieval models.

While the underlying evaluation methodology and metrics (such as NDCG@10) are well-known and robust, the integrity of existing benchmarks is often set back by the following problems:.

It has been revealed that the Generalization Gap. The current benchmark ecosystem inadvertently encourages "teaching to the test." When training data sources overlap with evaluation datasets, a model's score can become inflated, undermining a benchmark's integrity. This practice, whether intentional or not, is evident in the training datasets of several models. This creates a feedback loop where models are rewarded for memorizing test data rather than developing robust, generalizable capabilities.

Because of the above, models with a lower zero-shot score[1] may perform very well on the benchmark, without generalizing to new problems. For this reason, models with slightly lower benchmark performance and a higher zero-shot score are often recommended instead.

Misalignment with Today’s AI Applications. Many benchmarks are poorly aligned with the enterprise use cases that developers are building today. They often rely on academic datasets or on retrieval tasks derived from QA datasets, which, while useful in their own right, were not designed to evaluate retrieval and can fail to capture the distributional biases and complexities encountered in real-world retrieval scenarios. Benchmarks which do not possess these concerns are often too narrow, focusing on a single domain like code retrieval, making them unsuitable for evaluating general-purpose models.

In a recent development, today, we’re excited to introduce the Retrieval Embedding Benchmark (RTEB). Its goal is to create a new, reliable, high-quality benchmark that measures the true retrieval accuracy of embedding models.

To combat benchmark overfitting, RTEB implements a hybrid strategy using both open and private datasets:.

This hybrid approach encourages the development of models with broad, robust generalization. A model with a significant performance drop between the open and the private datasets would suggest overfitting, providing a clear signal to the community. This is already apparent with some models, which show a notable drop in performance on RTEB's private datasets.

It has been revealed that RTEB is designed with a particular emphasis on enterprise use cases. Instead of a complex hierarchy, it uses simple groups for clarity. A single dataset can belong to multiple groups (e.g., a German law dataset exists in both the "law" and "German" groups).

A complete list of the datasets can be found below. We initiative to continually update both the open as well as closed portion with different categories of datasets and actively encourage participation from the community; please open an problem on the MTEB repository on GitHub if you would like to suggest other datasets.

RTEB is launching today in beta. We believe building a robust benchmark is a community effort, and we initiative to evolve RTEB based on feedback from developers and researchers alike. We encourage you to share your thoughts, suggest new datasets, find concerns in existing datasets and help us build a more reliable standard for everyone. Please feel free to join the discussion or open an issue in the MTEB repository on Github.

To highlight areas for improvement we want to be transparent about RTEB's current limitations and our plans for the future.

Our goal is for RTEB to become a community-trusted standard for retrieval evaluation.

The RTEB leaderboard is available today on Hugging Face as a part of the new Retrieval section on the MTEB leaderboard. We invite you to check it out, evaluate your models, and join us in building a better, more reliable benchmark for the entire AI community.

Industry observers note that [1] Zero-shot score is the proportion of the evaluation set which the model provider have explicitly stated to have trained on. This typically only includes the training split.

Observed a fun fact: English-only models tend to get worse performance on closed datasets, while multilingual models are better at closed dataset.

Is it because the baseline, MTEB, is a benchmark merely in English, and RTEB is multilingual? It's natural that multilingual model get better performance on multilingual benchmark instead of English.

RTEB is by default multilingual, however it has an English subset (at the moment denoted as RTEB(eng, beta) or RTEB English on the leaderboard selection menu).

There is also an argument that multilingual models are more robust to phenomena such as code-switching and foreign terms.

Are you planning on releasing an academic paper on RTEB?

The discussion about English-only versus multilingual subsets shows why a single retrieval average can hide crucial differences. Would it be feasible to report lexical baselines alongside embedding models per language, including identifier-heavy and paraphrase-heavy slices? We recently evaluated BM25 plus semantic reranking on a small English-only workload: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That result doesn't tell us how the approach would perform on RTEB's multilingual or private datasets.

RTEB leaderboard have bm25 and some other baseline models https://leaderboard.mteb.org/benchmark/RTEB(beta)?pin=mteb%252Fbaseline-bm25s.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, draper Associates, Planetary VC and Epoch VC also participated. The seed followed a pre-seed angel round of less than $1 million. Maple intends to raise a Series A in the first half of 2027, according to the report, which attributed that timetable to investor interest.

According to recent reports, maple’s product pitch is to enforce privacy through system design rather than rely only on a provider’s data policy. On its official site, Maple states open models operate inside encrypted enclaves and conversations have end-to-end encryption; it also says those conversations are not used to train AI or shared with advertisers by design.

CEO Mark Suman described a process intended to keep Maple from seeing raw user data in flight or at rest. Information is encrypted on the user’s device using a password known only to that user, decrypted for processing inside a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) — a server with hardware encryption — and encrypted again before being returned. The models run in these environments in a U.S. data center, with European support provided through a partner operating a server in Europe. Suman remarked customers can inspect the open-source code and verify what runs on the servers: “They can audit everything themselves and know how their data is being handled.”.

Maple Chat combines long-form conversations, document analysis and web search across mobile and desktop apps. Users can select open models from providers including OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek and Kimi, or switch between a quicker option and a more powerful one.

Suman previously spent six years at Apple, where he worked on AI and machine learning with a focus on computer vision. Co-founder and CTO Anthony Ronning has a background in defense technology, security and networking. Ronning started the predecessor privacy-focused fintech in 2023; Suman joined him in August 2024, and Maple’s mobile product became public in January 2025.

The new Maple Work desktop app moves beyond chat by operating the computer and completing tasks across local files, applications and a web browser. An integration store connects services such as Gmail and calendars. For supported tools such as Claude and Codex, Work can use the Agent Client Protocol, a connection for compatible AI tools, to create a subagent while limiting shared information to what the task requires.

Maple is targeting small businesses with Work. Its stated strategy for 2027 is to begin enterprise pilots offering the company’s version of zero data retention: most customer data is not retained, while information that must be kept is encrypted. Maple is completing SOC 2 compliance work and security audits ahead of that expansion.

The company earns revenue through subscriptions. Its pricing page lists a free tier, Pro at $20 per month, Max at $100, Max+ at $200 and Team at $30 per user per month. Pro includes $20 of monthly usage, while Max and Max+ include $200 and $400; Chat, Work and API usage share one balance, and additional usage is never charged automatically.

Recent findings suggest that maple declined to disclose its registered customer count but reported 60-fold growth over the three months preceding the report. The Austin- and San Francisco-based startup has four employees and is actively hiring.

For Maple, the central test is whether the same encrypted architecture can support persistent cloud agents and enterprise security requirements while preserving the privacy boundary on which its product pitch depends.

OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.
  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • OpenAI has detailed Pando, a latest backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

OpenAI has detailed Pando, a latest backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.

Sources indicate that pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.

Rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the new branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.

OpenAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.

Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.

Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source).

Recent findings suggest that for fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.

Sources indicate that background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.

Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source).

The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.

In a recent development, both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.

Git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI indicates some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.

Industry observers note that for the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter.
  • Recent findings suggest that enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017.
  • In a recent development, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year our hardware is a little more powerful, our models a little smarter for each parameter. In 2025, it is more feasible than ever to run truly competitive models on-device. dots.ocr, a 3B parameter OCR model from RedNote, surpasses Gemini 2.5 Pro in OmniDocBench, making OCR a truly no compromises on-device use case. Running models on-device is certainly appealing to developers: no smuggling API keys, zero cost, and no network required. However, if we want these models to run on-device, we need to be mindful of the limited compute and power budgets.

Recent findings suggest that enter the Neural Engine, Apple's custom AI accelerator that has shipped with every Apple device since 2017. This accelerator is designed for high performance whilst sipping battery power. Some of our testing has found the Neural Engine to be 12x more power efficient than CPU, and 4x more power efficient than GPU.

In a recent development, whilst this all sounds very appealing, unfortunately the Neural Engine is only accessible through Core ML, Apple's closed source ML framework. Furthermore, even just converting a model from PyTorch to Core ML can present some challenges, and without a preconverted model or some knowledge of the sharp edges it can be arduous for developers. Luckily, Apple also offers MLX, a more modern and flexible ML framework that targets the GPU (not the Neural Engine), and can be used in conjunction with Core ML.

In this three part series, we will provide a reasoning trace of how we converted dots.ocr to run on-device, using a combination of CoreML and MLX. This process should be applicable to many other models, and we hope that this will help highlight the ideas and tools needed for developers looking to run their own models on-device.

Sources indicate that to follow along, clone the repo. You'll need uv and hf installed to run the setup command:.

If you just want to skip ahead and use the converted model, you can download it here.

Converting from PyTorch to CoreML is a two step process:.

Whilst we do have a few knobs we can tweak for step 2, most of our control is in step 1, the graph we feed to coremltools.

Following the programmers litany of make it work, make it right, make it fast, we will first focus on getting the conversion working on GPU, in FLOAT32, and with static shapes. Once we have this working, we can dial down the precision and try and move to the Neural Engine.

Sources indicate that dots.OCR consists of two key components: A 1.2B parameter vision encoder trained from scratch, based on the NaViT architecture, and a Qwen2.5-1.5B backbone. We will be using CoreML to run the vision encoder, and MLX to run the LM backbone.

In a recent development, in order to convert a model, it's best to understand the structure and function before getting started. Looking at the original vision modelling file here, we can see that the vision encoder is similar to the QwenVL family. Like many vision encoders, the vision encoder for dots works on a patch basis, in this case 14x14 patches. The dots vision encoder is capable of processing videos and batches of images. This gives us an opportunity to simplify by only processing a single image at a time. This approach is frequent in on-device apps, where we convert a model that provides the essential functions and iterate if we want to process multiple images.

When kicking off the conversion process, it's best to start with a minimal viable model. This means removing any bells and whistles that are not strictly necessary for the model to function. In our case, dots has many different attention implementations available for both the vision encoder and the LM backbone. CoreML has lots of infrastructure oriented around the scaled_dot_product_attention operator, which they introduced in iOS 18. We can simplify the model by removing all of the other attention implementations and just focusing on simple sdpa (not the memory efficient variant) for now, commit here.

Once we've done this, we see a scary warning message when we load the model:.

The model doesn't require Sliding Window Attention to function, so we can happily move on.

Using torch.jit.trace is still the most mature method for converting models to CoreML. We usually encapsulate this in a simple harness that allows you to modify the compute units used and the precision selected.

You can check out the initial harness here. If we run the following on the original code implementation:.

We should bump into the first (of many) issues.

It is rare that a model will convert first time. Often, you will need to progressively make changes further and further down the execution graph until you reach the final node.

Our first issue is the following error:.

Luckily this error gives us quite a bit of information. We can look at the VisionRotaryEmbedding layer and see the following code:.

Industry observers note that although torch.arange has a dtype argument, coremltools ignores this for arange and always outputs int32. We can simply add a cast after the arange to fix this issue, commit here.

After fixing this, running the conversion again leads us to our next issue at repeat_interleave:.

Whilst this error is less informative, we only have a single call to repeat_interleave in our vision encoder:.

cu_seqlens is used for masking variable length sequences in flash_attention_2. It's derived from the grid_thw tensor, which represents time, height and width. Since we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove this call, commit here.

Onto the next! This time, we get a more cryptic error:.

This is again due to the masking logic to handle variable length sequences. Since we are only processing a single image (not a video or batch of images), we don't really need attention masking at all! Therefore, we can just use a mask of all True. To prepare ourselves for the Neural Engine conversion, we also switch from using a boolean mask to a float mask of all zeros, as the Neural Engine does not support bool tensors commit here.

It has been revealed that with all of this done, the model should now successfully convert to CoreML! However, when we run the model, we get the following error:.

This reshape could be in multiple places! Luckily, we can use a previous warning message to help us track down the issue:.

It has been revealed that most ML compilers do not like dynamic control flow. Luckily for us, as we are only processing a single image, we can simply remove the loop and process the single h, w pair, commit here.

And there we have it! If we run the conversion again, we should see that the model successfully converts and matches the original PyTorch precision:.

Recent findings suggest that now that we've got the model working, let's evaluate the size and performance. The good news is the model is working, the bad news is that it's over 5GB! This is completely untenable for on device deployment! To benchmark the computation time, we can use the built in XCode tooling by calling:.

which will launch the XCode inspector for the model. After clicking + Performance Report and launching a report on all compute devices, you should see something like the following:.

Over a second for a single forward pass of the vision encoder! We have lots of more work.

In the third part, we will dive deep into the optimizations required to get this model running on the Neural Engine, including quantization and dynamic shapes.

Breaking: BigCodeArena: Judging code generations end to end with code executions

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult.
  • Inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces.
  • The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that evaluating the quality of AI-generated code is notoriously difficult. While humans can easily spot whether a piece of code "looks right," determining if it actually works correctly, handles edge cases properly, and produces the intended result requires running and testing it. This is why today, we're thrilled to announce BigCodeArena -- the first human-in-the-loop platform for evaluating code generation models through execution.

Inspired by LMArena for LLMs, we've built a platform that allows anyone to compare code generation models side-by-side, but with a crucial difference: you can actually run the code and see what it produces. Just submit a coding task, watch two different models generate solutions, execute both programs, and vote on which model produced better results. The outcomes are organized into a leaderboard that displays the community's highest-rated models.

The field of code generation has long struggled with reliable evaluation methods. Traditional benchmarks like HumanEval test code against predefined test cases, but these represent only a tiny fraction of real-world programming tasks. Human evaluation platforms exist for general chatbots, but they fall short for code: reading raw source code and mentally simulating its execution is cognitively demanding and error-prone, especially for longer programs or complex UI applications.

You ask two AI models to build a responsive photo gallery website. Both generate code that looks syntactically correct. But which one is actually better? Without running the code, it's nearly impossible to tell. One might produce a beautiful, functional grid layout, while the other might have subtle bugs or poor styling that only become apparent when rendered in a browser.

This observation led us to a key insight: execution feedback is essential for humans to judge code quality reliably. That's exactly what BigCodeArena provides.

BigCodeArena extends the Chatbot Arena framework with powerful features specifically designed for code evaluation:.

Every code snippet generated by models is automatically executed in isolated sandbox environments. Whether it's a Python script, a React web app, a PyGame game, or a C++ algorithm, you can see the actual output, not just the source code.

We currently support 10 languages (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, HTML, C, C++, Java, Go, Rust, and Markdown) and 8 execution environments:.

Unlike static code comparison, you can actually interact with the generated applications:.

Real programming isn't one-and-done. BigCodeArena supports multi-turn interactions, allowing you to refine requirements, ask for features to be added, or request bug fixes -- just like working with a real coding assistant.

Since launching in February 2025, BigCodeArena has collected over 14,000 conversations from more than 500 unique customers, with 4,700+ high-quality preference votes comparing 10 frontier LLMs.

Our people have explored remarkably diverse coding scenarios:.

Sources indicate that python dominates with over 4,000 conversations, followed by JavaScript/TypeScript (3,359), HTML (1,601), and C++ (642). Among frameworks, direct Python interpreters lead usage (6,000 sessions), with React (2,729), Core Web (1,574), Streamlit (1,254), and PyGame (1,087) also seeing heavy use.

Recent findings suggest that most interactions are focused and efficient: 76% of conversations consist of just 2 turns (one request, one response), with a mean conversation length of 4.12 messages. However, the platform supports extended multi-turn debugging sessions when needed, with some conversations exceeding 10 turns as users refine complex applications.

From our 14K conversations, we filtered for high-quality pairwise comparisons: conversations with at least two turns and actual code execution. This yielded 4,731 voting samples, with each evaluated model receiving at least 700 votes. We aggregate these votes into Elo ratings using the Bradley-Terry model, which estimates the probability that one model beats another based on head-to-head comparisons.

To ensure robust rankings, we use 100 bootstrap resamples to construct 95% confidence intervals, so we can identify statistically significant performance differences between models.

We evaluate models under three settings to control for different factors:.

Rankings remain remarkably consistent across all three settings, revealing clear performance tiers:.

Recent findings suggest that top Tier: o3-mini and o1-mini consistently lead with the highest Elo ratings and tight confidence intervals. These models maintain top performance regardless of environment or language constraints, showing strong robustness across coding scenarios. Claude-3.5-Sonnet follows closely, particularly excelling when language is controlled.

Industry observers note that mid Tier: GPT-4o, o1, and Gemini-2.0-Pro/Flash form a competitive middle tier. GPT-4o highlights some sensitivity to language matching, suggesting room for improvement in multilingual consistency.

Open Source Models: Qwen2.5 variants and Llama-3.3-70B lag behind frontier proprietary models, highlighting the performance gap that remains between leading closed and open models.

Recent findings suggest that figure: Overall win rate heatmaps (percentage of all pairwise comparisons won) of each model in the sessions across languages (left) and execution environments (right). For each category, we only keep models that appear in at least 3 conversation sessions.

Breaking down performance by programming language reveals interesting patterns:.

Analyzing win rates by execution environment reveals how models handle different runtime contexts:.

Robust Performers: o3-mini maintains consistently strong performance across React, Streamlit, Gradio, Core Web, and PyGame, demonstrating excellent environmental adaptability.

Stable but Selective: Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Gemini-2.0-Flash show generally stable performance but with reduced win rates in complex UI-heavy environments like Vue and Mermaid.

In a recent development, framework-Specific Weaknesses: Qwen2.5 models, while competitive in some web frameworks (Core Web, React), struggle significantly with interactive and visualization-oriented environments like PyGame, Vue, and Mermaid. These environments often require precise handling of control flow, graphics rendering, and package dependencies.

Industry observers note that these results highlight an important insight: aggregate Elo scores don't tell the whole story. Some models remain brittle under specific runtime constraints, and execution environment matters significantly for real-world deployment.

To advance research beyond crowdsourced evaluation, we're releasing two complementary benchmarks:.

It has been revealed that building on our 4,700+ preference votes, BigCodeReward tests how well LLMs can judge code quality when acting as reward models. The key finding? Execution results dramatically improve judgment accuracy.

When models can see execution outputs (screenshots of web apps, game visuals, program logs), their alignment with human preferences increases substantially:.

This reinforces our core thesis: you can't reliably judge code without running it -- and this applies to both humans and AI judges.

Inspired by Arena-Hard-Auto, AutoCodeArena provides a scalable way to evaluate latest models without waiting for thousands of human votes. We carefully selected 600 representative prompts from our crowdsourced data, spanning all programming topics and frameworks.

Using automated LLM judges (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) to evaluate code execution results against a GPT-4.1 baseline, we can rapidly benchmark new models. This approach enables weekly leaderboard updates as new models are released.

Our automated benchmark evaluated 20+ cutting-edge models, including recently released systems:.

Figure: Win rates of recent LLMs on AutoCodeArena against a GPT-4.1 baseline, judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet. The 50% mark represents parity with GPT-4.1. Models above this line outperform the baseline, while those below underperform. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals. Note: Claude-3.7-Sonnet is excluded from rankings to avoid self-judgment bias, and GPT-4.1 appears only as the reference baseline.

The results show that while proprietary models maintain an edge, open-source models are rapidly closing the gap, with some approaching GPT-4.1-level performance.

BigCodeArena is open to everyone -- no account required! Visit https://huggingface.co/spaces/bigcode/arena to:.

Whether you're building a React dashboard, creating a PyGame game, solving algorithmic challenges, or generating creative visualizations, BigCodeArena lets you see which models truly deliver.

Following the BigCode Project's commitment to transparency, we're releasing:.

We envision BigCodeArena as a long-term project that evolves with the community:.

Industry observers note that evaluating code isn't like evaluating text -- you need to run it, test it, and interact with it. BigCodeArena makes this possible at scale, combining human judgment with real execution feedback to create the most reliable evaluation platform for code generation models.

Join us in building the future of code generation evaluation. Write a prompt, compare the models, and vote for your favorite. Your feedback helps the entire community understand which models truly deliver on the promise of AI-assisted programming.

We'd love to hear your feedback! Connect with us on GitHub, join discussions in the Hugging Face Space community tab, or reach out to the BigCode Project at contact@bigcode-project.org.

We thank Leandro von Werra for his valuable suggestions and feedback on the blog.

That explanation places leadership continuity with the executives already running NVIDIA’s businesses, instead of a formal process for designating his replacement.

In its reinstatement announcement on November 23, 2026, NVIDIA said the board voted unanimously to restore Huang as president, CEO and director after concluding that it was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead. Harvey Jones remained chair, and Kress continued as CFO.

According to recent reports, the board said it received input from senior levels of the US government and, based on that input, was confident the reinstatement posed no national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he gave the board assurances and “made the deal” to restore Huang.

It has been revealed that the tech giant’s announcement said the independent-director committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion, with independent counsel assisting and Huang committed to cooperating. NVIDIA has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee composed solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The tech giant is also starting a search for a chief compliance officer who will oversee compliance across NVIDIA and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. NVIDIA will continue cooperating with government investigations and inquiries.

Industry observers note that huang’s first meeting therefore paired an apology with a case for continuity through NVIDIA’s existing leadership structure. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.
  • Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News CNCF Research Reveals Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. Latest research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

It has been revealed that the report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

Industry observers note that the research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

According to recent reports, the survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates fresh risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

Sources indicate that the survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain vital, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

In a recent development, for platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly notable infrastructure considerations.

The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that together AI made preemptible GPU compute generally available on Together GPU Clusters on November 24, 2026, covering Kubernetes and Slurm deployments in all regions.
  • Recent findings suggest that customers can add preemptible capacity when creating a cluster or to one already running.
  • The price does not move with a spot market or require a bid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that together AI made preemptible GPU compute generally available on Together GPU Clusters on November 24, 2026, covering Kubernetes and Slurm deployments in all regions. The interruptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute as standard nodes, at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate.

Recent findings suggest that customers can add preemptible capacity when creating a cluster or to one already running. The nodes draw from unused supply and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere. Standard nodes remain the default: they are provisioned synchronously and are never preempted, whereas preemptible nodes fill in asynchronously as spare capacity becomes available.

The price does not move with a spot market or require a bid. Usage is metered every one to two minutes and billed sub-hourly, so customers pay approximately for the minutes a node runs rather than a full hour. The fixed discount makes the rate predictable even though the requested capacity is not guaranteed.

The Together AI documentation distinguishes desired_preemptible_gpus from allocated_preemptible_gpus, so customers can see when live capacity falls short of the target. Targets must be set in multiples of eight GPUs. After a reclamation, the cluster retains its target and automatically provisions replacements as spare capacity returns, without another capacity request.

It has been revealed that reclamation starts with a drain window of at most five minutes and ends with node removal, regardless of whether work has finished. There is no minimum node lifetime. Those terms put recovery design at the center of the cost decision: a workload needs to tolerate losing a worker at any point, then resume when replacement capacity arrives.

Recent findings suggest that on Kubernetes, reclamation cordons the node, emits a TogetherPreemptionNotified warning and sends pods a SIGTERM shutdown signal. Workloads can set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to use up to the full drain window for checkpointing and exit; pods without that setting receive the Kubernetes default of 30 seconds. A together.ai/compute-class node label lets interruptible workers target preemptible nodes while coordinators, login pods and user-facing serving replicas remain on standard nodes.

In a recent development, on Slurm, preemptible and standard nodes share partitions and the same scheduling feature, so the scheduler cannot target preemptible nodes or keep a job off them. Jobs still running when a node is removed are killed, and only jobs submitted with --requeue are resubmitted. A requeued job can resume from its last checkpoint, but any work completed after that checkpoint is lost.

Together AI recommends the capacity for checkpointed or retryable work, including short experiments, configuration sweeps, fine-tuning, evaluations, distillation, batch inference and temporary inference bursts. For a sweep or internal inference spike, teams can raise the target and lower it afterward while keeping the cluster running, instead of holding standard capacity sized for peak demand. Multi-day runs without checkpoints, user-facing serving without fallback and workloads with strict service-level objectives are not suitable.

The company remarked it already uses preemptible clusters for internal research, development and testing, and non-critical production workloads, spreading spare capacity across product teams.

A cluster can consist entirely of preemptible nodes, but Together can reclaim all of them. Data on shared volumes persists, yet shared volumes and the Slurm control plane remain reachable while no nodes are running only in some regions and on a best-effort basis. Customers needing continuously reachable shared storage therefore need at least one standard node. Nodes cannot be converted between standard and preemptible types in place.

The launch turns Together’s spare GPU supply into a fixed-discount option for AI infrastructure teams. Its value depends on workload design: checkpoints, retry logic and standard-node fallback determine whether reclamation is a recoverable interruption or results in lost progress and unavailable service.

A compound AI approach to Indian personas grounded in real-world distributions.

Sources indicate that india represents one of the world's largest AI opportunities — with over 700 million internet users, a multitude of languages, and a rapidly growing developer ecosystem. Yet, most open datasets reflect Western norms and English-only contexts, creating a data gap that limits AI adoption in India's multilingual, multi-script environment.

In a recent development, today, we're releasing Nemotron-Personas-India, the first open synthetic dataset of Indic personas aligned to India's real-world demographic, geographic, and cultural distributions. Licensed under CC BY 4.0, this dataset offers a privacy-preserving, regulation-ready foundation for scaling AI systems that reflect Indian society—without relying on sensitive personal data.

Built with NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's enterprise-grade synthetic data generation microservice, Nemotron-Personas-India extends our global collection of Sovereign AI datasets. It builds on the success of our US and Japan persona datasets and includes new features designed specifically for India's culturally rich landscape.

This dataset integrates seamlessly with Nemotron models and other open-source LLMs, making it easy to fine-tune AI systems for Indian use cases—from multilingual chatbots to culturally-grounded specialized copilots.

This release complements our earlier suite of Hindi evaluation datasets — including ChatRAG-Hi, IFEval-Hi, MT-Bench-Hi, GSM8K-Hi, and BFCL-Hi — supporting a complete pipeline from synthetic data generation to rigorous model evaluation for Indian AI systems.

According to recent reports, produced using NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's microservice for synthetic data generation. This compound AI system enables generation with complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and supports multiple generation backends – the necessary tooling to scale a synthetic dataset of this size. We also leveraged the following models:.

This dataset was aligned to India’s official demographic distributions from the 2011 Census and expanded to include attributes essential for trustworthy AI training:.

No real names. No re-identification risk.

Sources indicate that all personas are fully synthetic. While grounded in real-world distributions from the 2011 Census and Parsed Indian Electoral Rolls data, no data is tied to any living or deceased individual. This ensures developers can safely train AI systems without privacy risks or regulatory barriers.

Built for India, Ready for the World.

Nemotron‑Personas‑India is designed for developers building Sovereign AI systems for the Indian market, as well as global teams looking to adapt models to India’s unique linguistic, cultural, and social context.

Most open datasets today reflect English-speaking, Western norms—limiting AI performance in India’s multilingual, multi-script, and demographically complex environments.

With Nemotron‑Personas‑India, teams can:.

India's 1.4 billion people speak hundreds of languages and live across vast cultural, economic, and geographic divides. India's National AI Portal estimates over 7,000 AI startups and research institutions are working to build locally relevant AI systems, and the Digital India initiative and government programs like IndiaAI are accelerating adoption.

But progress is constrained by a fundamental gap: high-quality, culturally grounded training data that reflects India's demographic reality. Without representative datasets, AI systems struggle with code-switching between English and Hindi, fail to understand regional occupational categories, and miss cultural context essential for trust and adoption.

The dataset improves diversity of synthetically-generated data, mitigates biases, and prevents model collapse (degradation caused by uncurated training on another model's outputs) by reflecting India's real geographic and demographic distributions.

Nemotron-Personas-India supports Indian model builders in developing Sovereign AI systems that incorporate important region-specific demographics and cultural context.

Want to build AI systems that understand India's culture, languages, and people?

Whether you're an Indian model builder developing Sovereign AI or a global developer seeking better regional adoption, Nemotron-Personas-India provides the authentic, privacy-safe foundation your applications need.

According to recent reports, download it. Fine-tune it. Build AI that understands India. If you’re ready to go deeper, an extended version of Nemotron-Personas-India (which includes e.g., first/last names, religion, and synthetic addresses) is available in NeMo Data Designer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that openTable confirmed on November 24, 2026, that it had agreed to acquire me&u, an Australian restaurant technology firm with voice AI, reservations and order-and-pay products. The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the proposed combination would pair OpenTable’s reservation and guest-experience business with me&u’s tools for ordering and payment, guest databases, waitlists, voice AI, private dining, events and table management. CEO Debby Soo said me&u’s platform was built for busy casual-dining businesses with complicated operations. For OpenTable, the deal would add operational software for the high-volume, multi-venue groups me&u serves.

On me&u’s reservations platform, the voice agent takes bookings and answers common questions, recognizes returning guests, routes VIP calls to staff and sends real-time transcripts to central teams. The tech giant claims the system handles 70% to 80% of calls, drawing on a human-reviewed Q&A bank that improves weekly.

Other AI features include an assistant that suggests actions, automated shift briefs and natural-language queries of booking data. Reservations and event spaces share one floor proposal, and group-level guest profiles carry visits, notes and dietary needs across venues. Taken together, those features show that the acquisition’s AI component extends beyond phone automation into booking, event and guest-management workflows.

The companies’ published figures illustrate the distribution opportunity: OpenTable helps more than 70,000 restaurants worldwide fill 2 billion seats a year, while me&u processes more than one million orders weekly and has more than 6,000 locations using its products worldwide.

me&u CEO Kim Teo mentioned: “Joining them means we can bring our tools to venues at a scale we couldn’t reach on our own—while adding more value than ever for our customers.”.

In a recent development, the companies already have a technical connection. me&u’s integration listing identifies OpenTable as a booking integration built by OpenTable, compatible with me&u’s Connect CRM and Grow products in Australia, Newly introduced Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States. That link provides a documented starting point for connecting reservations with guest-data and return-visit workflows.

OpenTable mentioned me&u customers will see no changes to products or pricing as a result of the announcement. Once the transaction closes, me&u is to operate as a standalone OpenTable division reporting to Soo, with Teo and the current key leaders continuing to run the business and me&u employees joining OpenTable. Any brand alignment in international markets outside Australia will be evaluated later.

The agreement gives OpenTable a path from reservations into AI-assisted daily operations. Regulatory approvals and closing conditions still govern the timing, while the existing integration and continuity commitments provide a defined base for bringing those tools to a broader restaurant network.

  • In a recent development, small models like SmolVLM are built for low-resource consumption, but they can be further optimized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the growing capability of large language models (LLMs), a fresh class of models has emerged: Vision Language Models (VLMs). These models can analyze images and videos to describe scenes, create captions, and answer questions about visual content.

Recent findings suggest that while running AI models on your own device can be difficult as these models are often computationally demanding, it also offers significant benefits: including improved privacy since your data stays on your machine, and enhanced speed and reliability because you're not dependent on an internet connection or external servers. This is where tools like Optimum Intel and OpenVINO come in, along with a small, efficient model like SmolVLM. In this blog post, we'll walk you through three easy steps to get a VLM running locally, with no expensive hardware or GPUs required (though you can run all the code samples from this blog post on Intel GPUs).

In a recent development, small models like SmolVLM are built for low-resource consumption, but they can be further optimized. In this blog post we will see how to optimize your model, to lower memory usage and speedup inference, making it more efficient for deployment on devices with limited resources.

To follow this tutorial, you need to install optimum and openvino, which you can do with:.

First, you will need to convert your model to the OpenVINO IR. There are multiple options to do it:.

According to recent reports, now it’s time to optimize your model. Quantization reduces the precision of the model weights and/or activations, leading to smaller, faster models. Essentially, it's a way to map values from a high-precision data type, such as 32-bit floating-point numbers (FP32), to a lower-precision format, typically 8-bit integers (INT8). While this process offers several key benefits, it can also impact in a potential loss of accuracy.

Optimum supports two main post-training quantization methods:.

Recent findings suggest that weight-only quantization means that only the weights are quantized but activations remain in their original precisions. As a result, the model becomes smaller and more memory-efficient, improving loading times. But since activations are not quantized, inference speed gains are limited. Weight-only quantization is a simple first step since it usually doesn’t result in significant accuracy degradation.

Since OpenVINO 2024.3, if the model's weight have been quantized, the corresponding activations will also be quantized at runtime, leading to additional speedup depending on the device.

In order to run it, you will need to create a quantization configuration OVWeightQuantizationConfig as follows:.

With Static Quantization, both weights and activations are quantized before inference. To achieve the best estimate for the activation quantization parameters, we perform a calibration step. During this step, a small representative dataset is fed through the model. In our case, we will use 50 samples of the contextual dataset and will apply static quantization on the vision encoder while weight-only quantization will be applied on the rest of the model. Experiments show that applying static quantization on the vision encoder provides a noticeable performance improvement without significant accuracy degradation. Since the vision encoder is called only once per generation, the overall performance gain from applying static quantization on this component is lower than the gain achieved by optimizing more frequently used components like the language model. Nevertheless, this approach can be beneficial in certain scenarios. For example, when short answers are needed, especially with multiple images as input.

According to recent reports, quantizing activations adds small errors that can build up and affect accuracy, so careful testing afterward is key. More information and examples can be found in our documentation.

You can now run inference with your quantized model:.

If you have a recent Intel laptop, Intel AI PC, or Intel discrete GPU, you can load the model on GPU by adding device="gpu" when loading your model:.

Industry observers note that we also created a space so you can play with the original model and its quantized variants obtained by respectively applying weight-only quantization and mixed quantization. This demo runs on 4th Generation Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) processors.

To reproduce our results, check out our notebook.

In a recent development, we ran a benchmark to compare the performance of the PyTorch, OpenVINO, and OpenVINO 8-bit WOQ versions of the original model. The goal was to evaluate the impact of weight-only quantization on latency and throughput on Intel CPU hardware. For this test, we used a single image as input.

We measured the following metrics to evaluate the model's performance:.

Sources indicate that this benchmark demonstrates how small, optimized multimodal models, like SmolVLM2-256M, perform on Intel CPUs across different configurations. According to the tests, the PyTorch version shows high latency, with a time to first token (TTFT) of over 5s with a decoding throughput of 0.7 tokens/s. Simply converting the model with Optimum and running it on OpenVINO drastically reduces the time to first token (TTFT) to 0.42s (x12 speedup) and raises throughput to 47 tokens/s (x65). Applying 8-bit weight-only quantization further reduces TTFT (x1.7) and increases throughput (x1.4), while also reducing model size and improving efficiency.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perplexity published an internal-search guide on November 24, 2026, urging separate permission and citation tests for AI-generated answers and citing Maeil Business Newspaper’s reported gains of 44.3% more searches and 22.6% more people using search after the publisher added AI answers.

Industry observers note that the guide addresses two environments: visitors searching a company’s website and employees looking through workplace material such as policies, contracts and meeting notes. In both, an internal search engine indexes selected content, matches queries against that material and ranks the results, while the organization controls what is included and how matches are ordered.

Its five-part framework covers index scope, query interpretation, access rights, result ranking and correction of failed searches. The recommended sequence begins with the search already built into ecommerce, content-management and workplace systems. A purchase is framed around a specific missing capability, while custom development is reserved for requirements no available tool can satisfy and only when a team can maintain the system.

Sources indicate that generated answers create a distinct access-control problem. A response can use information from a document even when that document never appears as a listed result, so checking only visible links can miss content the searcher is not permitted to open. Perplexity’s suggested test uses an account with a fresh hire’s permissions to search for both accessible and restricted material, including previews and generated responses. Access to a test document is then withdrawn and the exercise repeated.

Sources indicate that ranking needs the same scrutiny inside the answer. A results page can surface the current, approved policy while the generated response relies on an older copy. A separate exercise uses ten employee questions whose answers are already known. The responsible team identifies the approved document for each one, and the reviewer checks where it appears, whether the AI answer cites it and whether the summary retains the policy’s conditions and exceptions.

For ongoing evaluation, the guide calls for a baseline set of 20 genuine employee questions, each run in its original wording. Teams are told to distinguish failures caused by missing content, disconnected sources, permissions, query wording and ranking. Monthly reviews of no-result searches and flagged answers should lead to another run of that test set, because a log showing that an answer was delivered does not show whether it was correct.

Internal Knowledge Search provides Perplexity’s own Enterprise example. Administrators can place up to 500 files in a shared organization repository, and users can select Web, Org Files or Web + Org Files, or choose None for a response without external sources. Answers based on organization files include inline citations that let users open or download the underlying documents, according to Perplexity’s product documentation.

According to recent reports, the repository supports XLSX, PPTX, DOCX, PDF and CSV files up to 50 MB each. PNG and JPEG images are not supported for Internal Knowledge Search but can be attached directly to a query, while video files are indexed through audio transcription. Perplexity also warns that language-model-generated titles and summaries may contain inaccuracies and points users to the original file content when errors appear.

Industry observers note that project uploads remain outside the organization-wide repository. Only consumers in the same organization can be invited to a Project, and its files are limited to the creator and invited collaborators. A separate direct-attachment route allows up to ten files per session and deletes them after seven days; organization files remain until an administrator removes or updates them.

The customer example is Maeil Business Newspaper, which publishes more than 600 articles daily across 14 categories. Its earlier on-site search directed readers to relevant stories but still required them to open several articles to assemble an answer. Maeil implemented Perplexity’s Sonar API to synthesize information across articles and cite the original stories, according to a Perplexity customer case study. Sonar API is now part of Agent API.

Maeil’s AI Task Force at Maekyung Media Group led onboarding and jointly developed deployment strategies with Perplexity. The case study also claims Maeil planned to recommend follow-up questions based specifically on its existing content.

Industry observers note that maeil’s reported adoption gives the guide a concrete customer example, while its checklists show the operating work behind one. For enterprise teams, AI answers add continuing responsibilities for source ownership, access control and correctness checks after deployment.

Sources indicate that intel and Hugging Face collaborated to demonstrate the real-world value of upgrading to Google’s latest C4 Virtual Machine (VM) running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors (codenamed Granite Rapids (GNR)). We specifically wanted to benchmark improvements in the text generation performance of OpenAI GPT OSS Large Language Model(LLM).

Sources indicate that the results are in, and they are impressive, demonstrating a 1.7x improvement in Total Cost of Ownership(TCO) over the previous-generation Google C3 VM instances. The Google Cloud C4 VM instance further resulted in:.

Sources indicate that GPT OSS is a common name for an open-source Mixture of Experts (MoE) model released by OpenAI. An MoE model is a deep neural network architecture that uses specialized “expert” sub-networks and a “gating network” to decide which experts to use for a given input. MoE models allow you to scale your model capacity efficiently without linearly scaling compute costs. They also allow for specialization, where different “experts” learn different skills, allowing them to adapt to diverse data distributions.

Even with very large parameters, only a small subset of experts is activated per token, making CPU inference viable.

Intel and Hugging Face collaborated to merge an expert execution optimization (PR #40304) to eliminate redundant computation where every expert processed all tokens to transformers. This optimization directed each expert to run only on the tokens it is routed to, removing FLOPs waste and improving utilization.

We benchmarked GPT OSS under a controlled, repeatable generation workload to isolate architectural differences (GCP C4 VMs on Intel Xeon 6 processors (GNR) vs GCP C3 VMs on 4th Gen Intel Xeon Processors (SPR)) and MoE execution efficiency. The focus is steady‑state decoding (per‑token latency) and end‑to‑end normalized throughput with increasing batch size while keeping sequence lengths fixed. All runs use static KV cache and SDPA attention for determinism.

#195066. AI for Food Allergies
