📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weaknesses in the ground-based infrastructure supporting satellite services are becoming more consequential as a fresh space race gathers pace.
  • The satellites circling Earth may seem far removed from the reach of cyberattackers, but the ground-based networks and infrastructure supporting them have long offered plenty of ways in.
  • In a newly introduced analysis of cyber threats emerging around the booming space ecosystem, Recorded Future's Insikt Group warned that in 2025 alone, organizations and nations around the world placed 4,517 satellites in orbit; 87% of them are commercially owned, contributing to a $686 billion space economy that is growing rapidly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weaknesses in the ground-based infrastructure supporting satellite services are becoming more consequential as a fresh space race gathers pace.

The satellites circling Earth may seem far removed from the reach of cyberattackers, but the ground-based networks and infrastructure supporting them have long offered plenty of ways in. That exposure is now becoming increasingly consequential as the number of satellites in orbit and the services depending on them grow rapidly.

In a newly introduced analysis of cyber threats emerging around the booming space ecosystem, Recorded Future's Insikt Group warned that in 2025 alone, organizations and nations around the world placed 4,517 satellites in orbit; 87% of them are commercially owned, contributing to a $686 billion space economy that is growing rapidly.

Satellite services now underpin a growing range of everyday services and critical operations, from communications and navigation to shipping and infrastructure monitoring. As dependence on them grows, so does the potential fallout from a cyberattack that disrupts them, Recorded Future researchers warned. The growing militarization of space and the emergence of orbital AI data centers, such as those that Google and SpaceX are exploring with Project Suncatcher and Starmind, respectively, introduces another layer of risk, the company noted.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry.

Recorded Future pointed to several incidents where attackers exploited weaknesses in the ground-based systems supporting satellite communications to cause widespread disruption. One of the most consequential examples was in February 2022, just before Russia invaded Ukraine. Russian attackers used a destructive, data-wiping malware, dubbed AcidRain, to disable tens of thousands of modems connected to Viasat's KA-SAT satellite broadband network, after first gaining access to the network through a misconfigured VPN appliance. The disruption affected Ukrainian military communications as well as ordinary customers across Europe. In Germany, some 5,800 wind turbines lost their remote monitoring connections.

In a recent development, A similar pattern emerged in attacks against Iran's commercial shipping fleet in 2025, when a group calling itself Lab-Dookhtegan disabled communications aboard dozens of tankers and cargo vessels. The attackers reportedly gained access through Fanava Group, an Iranian IT provider serving the fleet, and obtained administrator-level control of shipboard Linux systems. They used that access to disable satellite communications software and software for identifying and tracking ship movements.

In a recent development, recorded Future also pointed to an incident last August, where an oil tanker lost communications for about 30 hours after attackers seemingly compromised the ship's onboard network. Investigators focused on the satellite terminals aboard the ship and the remote-maintenance systems connecting them to shore as possible points of entry, the company noted.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering.

Industry observers note that "In none of these cases did anyone touch an object in orbit. The attackers went for the vendor, the terminal, the management plane," Recorded Future explained.

Sources indicate that even as geopolitical rivalries fuel a fresh space race, the basics remain broken. "Every satellite has a terrestrial address: the ground stations that command it, the links that carry its telemetry, the user terminals at the edge, and the software supply chain behind it all. That is where attackers go, because that is where the doors are," according to the firm.

Industry observers note that its report dovetails with research by teams at the University of California, San Diego, and the University of Maryland. Using a satellite dish costing just $800, the researchers found that roughly half of the geostationary satellites they could observe were transmitting data unencrypted. The exposed traffic included telecommunications backhaul, corporate communications, and military data.

The US National Security Agency has also warned of the expanding attack surface created by the proliferation of low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellite networks. In a joint advisory with the Australian Signals Directorate and other international partners, the NSA examined security risks across the satellite communications ecosystem. This included satellites, ground stations and control centers, user terminals, end-user devices, radio links, and third-party suppliers. The agencies highlighted threats ranging from radio-frequency jamming, signal spoofing, and interception to weaknesses in ground infrastructure and user equipment.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool.

In a recent development, "The ground segment is highly exposed to cyber threats due to its extensive connectivity with terrestrial networks," the NSA and its partners warned. "Ground segments are typically the most interconnected and vulnerable points in a space system." Highlighted risks included malware injection, social engineering, DoS attacks, identity-based attacks and poor user practices.

To address these risks, the advisory recommended continuous monitoring of ground systems, stronger endpoint security and access controls, and technical safeguards such as frequency-hopping signals, backup communications paths, and anti-jamming antennas to protect satellite links.

Recorded Future's own recommendations are for all stakeholders to begin treating space infrastructure as critical national infrastructure, holding vendors to stronger security standards, and implementing basic measures like encryption for satellite communication.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

It has been revealed that over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

Industry observers note that jai previously served as senior editor at Computerworld, where he covered information security and data-privacy complications. His work has also appeared in CSO Online, InformationWeek, The Christian Science Monitor Passcode, The Economic Times, and other publications.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that at 01:25 UTC this morning I pulled the API of HyperRadar — the Hyperliquid smart-money tracker I run. The wallet sitting at #1 on the weekly leaderboard, 0xf5d81a…ec3ad53, held a 5.10 BTC long with an entry of $59,406.

Two minutes later I pulled again: 5.51 BTC. By the time its wallet page finished loading: 6.40 BTC. Over roughly ten minutes, while BTC traded around $59,400 — down 3.46% on the day, from $61,533 — this wallet kept buying the dip, coin by coin.

Industry observers note that it has made $10.63M in the last 24 hours. Not from holding. From churning $1.67B of volume. Here's what's inside the machine.

Context first. Yesterday, HyperRadar's top-wallet flow board — the aggregate open positions of the weekly top-5 — was 100% short BTC: $17.5M in shorts, exactly $0 in longs, held straight into a +3.9% rally day. That was a losing stance.

It has been revealed that overnight the 7-day window rolled. A completely latest top-5 took the board — all five tagged "Hot Hand" (profitable in 3 of 3 measured windows), with weekly PnL between +$9.99M and +$12.59M. And their book is the mirror image of yesterday's: $20.40M in BTC longs, $0 in shorts. The alt exposure stays short-only: SOL $11.26M short, ZEC $7.03M, HYPE $2.79M, XRP $2.70M — zero longs on any of them.

According to recent reports, so "smart money flipped long" is partly cohort rotation: the leaderboard rolled, and the new top five was already positioned the other way. Which is its own kind of signal.

Recent findings suggest that read those together. Roughly 90% of this account's all-time profit was printed in the last 30 days. Its visible inventory is tiny: the largest single position is about $380K of BTC at 3x, and the next ones down are ETH (22.16), SOL (75.27), HYPE (6.21) — positions whose unrealized PnL column reads like pocket change: +$77, -$8, +$2, -$0.45. Nobody makes $10.6M a day holding positions like that. The money is in the round-trips: quote both sides, capture spread and flow, keep inventory near zero, repeat.

In a recent development, it's simultaneously long BTC, ETH, SOL, HYPE and short BNB, ARB, DOGE, SUI, WLD, NEAR, ONDO, ENA in micro clips. The direction of any single position barely matters — the churn is the business.

One more detail from the data: the wallet page shows just $1.59M of live account value in the active margin account, while the leaderboard snapshot lists account value around $104M (the 7d ROI math implies a ~$103M PnL base). Whether the difference is vault parking, subaccount splits, or snapshot lag, the effect is the same: this bot runs its strategy with a sliver of its capital margined at any moment. That's textbook market-maker capital efficiency.

The wallet actually carrying that $20.4M BTC long isn't the bot — it's 0xecb63…2b82b00, all-time PnL +$232.77M. Its structure is an old-school directional spread:.

BTC bleeds; alts bleed harder. The short shelf is up about $880K combined right now, covering the long leg's -$104K several times over. It's a relative-value bet — BTC outperforming the alt market — sized so the shorts pay for the dip. Today that structure ran exactly on script: 24h PnL +$2.57M.

The next time someone tells you "whales are all long" or "whales are all short" — check which window, which wallets, and which week. The aggregate flips more often than the narrative does.

Latest Update: Supercharge your OCR Pipelines with Open Models

📅 21 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We have added Chandra and OlmOCR-2 to this blog, as well as OlmOCR Scores of the models 🫡.
  • TL;DR: The rise of powerful vision-language models has transformed document AI.
  • Sources indicate that by the end, you’ll know how to choose the right OCR model, start building with it, and gain deeper insights into document AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have added Chandra and OlmOCR-2 to this blog, as well as OlmOCR Scores of the models 🫡.

TL;DR: The rise of powerful vision-language models has transformed document AI. Each model comes with unique strengths, making it tricky to choose the right one. Open-weight models offer better cost efficiency and privacy. To help you get started with them, we’ve put together this guide.

Sources indicate that by the end, you’ll know how to choose the right OCR model, start building with it, and gain deeper insights into document AI. Let’s go!

Industry observers note that optical Character Recognition (OCR) is one of the earliest and longest running challenges in computer vision. Many of AI’s first practical applications focused on turning printed text into digital form.

Recent findings suggest that with the surge of vision-language models (VLMs), OCR has advanced significantly. Recently, many OCR models have been developed by fine-tuning existing VLMs. But today’s capabilities extend far beyond OCR: you can retrieve documents by query or answer questions about them directly. Thanks to stronger vision features, these models can also handle low-quality scans, interpret complex elements like tables, charts, and images, and fuse text with visuals to answer open-ended questions across documents.

Recent models transcribe texts into a machine-readable format.The input can include:.

OCR models convert them into machine-readable text that comes in many different formats like HTML, Markdown and more.

On top of text, some models can also recognize:.

Some models know where images are inside the document, extract their coordinates, and insert them appropriately between texts. Other models generate captions for images and insert them where they appear. This is especially useful if you are feeding the machine-readable output into an LLM. Example models are OlmOCR by AllenAI, or PaddleOCR-VL by PaddlePaddle.

Models use different machine-readable output formats, such as DocTags, HTML or Markdown (explained in the next section Output Formats). The way a model handles tables and charts often depends on the output format they are using. Some models treat charts like images: they are kept as is. Other models convert charts into markdown tables or JSON, e.g., a bar chart can be converted as follows.

Similarly for tables, cells are converted into a machine-readable format while retaining context from headings and columns.

Different OCR models have different output formats. Briefly, here are the common output formats used by modern models.DocTag: DocTag is an XML-like format for documents that expresses location, text format, component-level information, and more. Below is an illustration of a paper parsed into DocTags. This format is employed by the open Docling models.

The right model depends on how you proposal to use its outputs:.

Documents can have complex structures, like multi-column text blocks and floating figures. Older OCR models handled these documents by detecting words and then the layout of pages manually in post-processing to have the text rendered in reading order, which is brittle. Modern OCR models, on the other hand, incorporate layout metadata to help preserve reading order and accuracy. This metadata is called “anchor”, it can come in bounding boxes. This process is also called as “grounding/anchoring” because it helps with reducing hallucination.

OCR models can either take in images and an optional text prompt, this depends on the model architecture and the pre-training setup.Some OCR models support prompt-based task switching, e.g. granite-docling can parse an entire page with the prompt “Convert this page to Docling” while it can also take prompts like “Convert this formula to LaTeX” along with a page full of formulas.Other models, however, are trained only for parsing entire pages, and they are conditioned to do this through a system prompt.For instance, OlmOCR by AllenAI takes a long conditioning prompt. Like many others, OlmOCR is technically an OCR fine-tuned version of a VLM (Qwen2.5VL in this case), so you can prompt for other tasks, but its performance will not be on par with the OCR capabilities.

We’ve seen an incredible wave of upcoming models this past year. Because so much work is happening in the open, these players build on and benefit from each other’s work. A great example is AllenAI’s release of OlmOCR, which not only released a model but also the dataset used to train it. With these, others can build upon them in new directions. The field is incredibly active, but it’s not always obvious which model to use.

Recent findings suggest that to make things a bit easier, we’re putting together a non-exhaustive comparison of some of our current favorite models. All of the models below are layout-aware and can parse tables, charts, and math equations. The full list of languages each model supports are detailed in their model cards, so make sure to check them if you’re interested. All models below have open-source license except for Chandra having OpenRAIL license and Nanonets license being unclear. The average scores are taken from model cards of Chandra, OlmOCR, evaluated on OlmOCR Benchmark, which is English-only. Many of the models in this collection have been fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-VL or Qwen3-VL, so we also provide Qwen3-VL model below as well.

While Qwen3-VL itself is a powerful and versatile vision-language model post-trained for document understanding and other tasks, it isn’t optimized for a single, universal OCR prompt. In contrast, the other models were fine-tuned using one or a few fixed prompts specifically designed for OCR tasks. So to use Qwen3-VL, we recommend experimenting with prompts.

Here’s a small demo for you to try some of the latest models and compare their outputs.

There’s no single best model, as every problem has different needs. Should tables be rendered in Markdown or HTML? Which elements should we extract? How should we quantify text accuracy and error rates? 👀While there are many evaluation datasets and tools, many don’t answer these questions. So we suggest using the following benchmarks:.

Industry observers note that when testing different OCR models, we've found that the performance across different document types, languages, etc., varies a lot. Your domain may not be well represented in existing benchmarks! To make effective use of this new generation of VLM-based OCR models we suggest aiming to collect a dataset of representative examples of your task domain and testing a few different models to compare their performance.

According to recent reports, most OCR models are small, having between 3B and 7B parameters; you can even find models with fewer than 1B parameters, like PaddleOCR-VL. However, the cost also depends on the availability of optimized implementations for specialized inference frameworks. For example, OlmOCR-2 comes with vLLM and SGLang implementations, and the cost per million pages is 178 dollars (assuming on H100 for $2.69/hour). DeepSeek-OCR can process 200k+ pages per day on a single A100 with 40GB VRAM. With napkin math, we see that the cost per million pages is more or less similar to OlmOCR (although it depends on your A100 provider). If your use case remains unaffected, you can also opt for quantized versions of the models. The cost of running open-source models heavily depends on the hourly cost of the instance and the optimizations the model includes, but it’s guaranteed to be cheaper than many closed-source models out there on a larger scale.

While the past year has seen a surge in open OCR models, this hasn't been matched by as many open training and evaluation datasets. An exception is AllenAI's olmOCR-mix-0225, which has been used to train at least 72 models on the Hub – likely more, since not all models document their training data.

Sharing more datasets could unlock even greater advances in open OCR models. There are several promising approaches for creating these datasets:.

It's worth noting that many such datasets exist but remain unused. Making them more readily available as 'training-ready' datasets carries a considerable potential for the open-source community.

We have received many questions about getting started with OCR models, so here are a few ways you can use local inference tools and host remotely with Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that most cutting-edge models come with vLLM support and transformers implementation. You can get more info about how to serve each from the models’ own cards. For convenience, we show how to infer locally using vLLM here. The code below can differ from model to model, but for most models it looks like the following.

And then you can query as follows using e.g. OpenAI client.

According to recent reports, transformers provides standard model definitions for easy inference and fine-tuning. Models available in transformers come with either official transformers implementation (model definitions within the library) or “remote code” implementations. Latter is defined by the model owners to enable easy loading of models into transformers interface, so you don’t have to go through the model implementation. Below is an example loading Nanonets model using transformers implementation.

MLXMLX is an open-source machine learning framework for Apple Silicon. MLX-VLM is built on top of MLX to serve vision language models easily. You can explore all the OCR models available in MLX format here. They also come in quantized versions.You can install MLX-VLM as follows.

Inference Endpoints for Managed DeploymentYou can deploy OCR models compatible with vLLM or SGLang on Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, either from a model repository “Deploy” option or directly through Inference Endpoints interface. Inference Endpoints serve the cutting-edge models in a fully managed environment with GPU acceleration, auto-scaling, and monitoring without manually managing the infrastructure.

Here is a simple method of deploying nanonets using vLLM as the inference engine.

You can learn more about it here.

Hugging Face Jobs for Batch Inference.

For many OCR applications, you want to do efficient batch inference, i.e., running a model across thousands of images as cheaply and efficiently as possible. A good approach is to use vLLM's offline inference mode. As discussed above, many recent VLM-based OCR models are supported by vLLM, which efficiently batches images and generates OCR outputs at scale.

To make this even easier, we've created uv-scripts/ocr, a collection of ready-to-run OCR scripts that work with Hugging Face Jobs. These scripts let you run OCR on any dataset without needing your own GPU. Simply point the script at your input dataset, and it will:.

For example, to run OCR on 100 images:.

The scripts handle all the vLLM configuration and batching automatically, making batch OCR accessible without infrastructure setup.

If you are interested in document AI, not just OCR, here are some of our recommendations.

In a recent development, visual document retrieval is to retrieve the most relevant top-k documents when given a text query. If you have previously worked with retriever models, the difference is that you search directly on a stack of PDFs. Aside from using them standalone, you can also build multimodal RAG pipelines by combining them with a vision language model (find how to do so here). You can find all of them on Hugging Face Hub.

There are two types of visual document retrievers, single-vector and multi-vector models. Single-vector models are more memory efficient and less performant; meanwhile, multi-vector models are more memory hungry and more performant. Most of these models often come with vLLM and transformers integrations, so you can index documents using them and then do a search easily using a vector DB.

In a recent development, if you have a task at hand that only requires answering questions based on documents, you can use some of the vision language models that had document tasks in their training tasks. We’ve observed people trying to convert documents into text and passing the output to LLMs, but if your document has a complex layout, and your converted document outputs charts and so on in HTML, or images are captioned incorrectly, the LLM will miss out. Instead, feed your document and query to one of the advanced vision language models like Qwen3-VL not to miss out on any context.

In this blog post, we wanted to give you an overview of how to pick your OCR model, existing cutting-edge models and capabilities, and the tools to get you started with OCR.If you want to learn more about OCR and vision language models, we encourage you to read the resources below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trong kỹ thuật phần mềm ứng dụng AI, các bài toán sinh học phân tử vốn được xem là lãnh địa riêng của những pipeline chuyên biệt với cấu trúc đầu vào khắt khe. Tuy nhiên, tiền ấn phẩm GPT-6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models vừa đặt lại giả định đó. Nghiên cứu cho thấy phiên bản GPT-6.2 cùng một mô hình nghiên cứu nội bộ mới nhất của OpenAI có thể tự thiết kế cấu trúc không gian 3D và trình tự axit amin cho protein chỉ bằng suy luận logic kết hợp viết và thực thi mã nguồn.

Trước đây, để tạo ra protein chặn tín hiệu giúp tế bào ung thư né tránh hệ miễn dịch hay thu giữ khí CO2 từ không khí, kỹ sư và nhà khoa học phải ghép nối nhiều mô hình chuyên ngành khác nhau. Điểm nghẽn lớn nhất của kiến trúc cũ nằm ở giao diện dữ liệu cứng nhắc: mỗi khi xuất hiện ràng buộc vật lý mới, hệ thống buộc phải sửa mã phần mềm hoặc huấn luyện lại.

Recent findings suggest that dòng GPT-6 tiếp cận vấn đề như một tác vụ giải ràng buộc đa ngành kết hợp lập trình. Thay vì gọi API tới các mô hình sinh học chuyên sâu, mô hình huy động tri thức toán học, vật lý, hóa học và sinh học để lập kế hoạch, sau đó tự viết code kiểm thử biến thể:.

Nhóm tác giả đã đánh giá khả năng của hệ thống trên 14 tác vụ tính toán khác nhau, đồng thời tiến hành kiểm chứng thực nghiệm trong phòng thí nghiệm cùng đối tác Onava. Kết quả đối chiếu cho thấy một mô hình nền tảng đa năng đã đạt mức cạnh tranh trực tiếp với các công cụ thiết kế protein chuyên ngành như RFdiffusion, đồng thời loại bỏ chi phí tái huấn luyện khi thay đổi đặc tả thiết kế.

Sự dịch chuyển từ công cụ chuyên biệt sang mô hình suy luận có khả năng viết mã mở ra hướng thiết kế phần mềm khoa học linh hoạt hơn hẳn:.

Sentence Transformers is joining Hugging Face!

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face.
  • SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning.
  • In a recent development, "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face. Hugging Face's Tom Aarsen has already been maintaining the library since late 2023 and will continue to lead the project. At its new home, Sentence Transformers will benefit from Hugging Face's robust infrastructure, including continuous integration and testing, ensuring that it stays up-to-date with the latest advancements in Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing.

Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning. Since its inception by Nils Reimers in 2019, Sentence Transformers has been widely adopted by researchers and practitioners for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including semantic search, semantic textual similarity, clustering, and paraphrase mining. After years of development and training by and for the community, over 16,000 Sentence Transformers models are publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub, serving more than a million monthly unique people.

In a recent development, "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab. Nils Reimers has made a very timely discovery and has produced not only outstanding research outcomes, but also a highly usable tool. This continues to impact generations of students and practitioners in natural language processing and AI. I would also like to thank all the users and especially the contributors, without whom this project would not be what it is today. And finally, I would like to thank Tom and Hugging Face for taking the project into the future.".

"We're thrilled to officially welcome Sentence Transformers into the Hugging Face family! Over the past two years, it’s been amazing to see this project grow to massive global adoption, thanks to the incredible foundation from the UKP Lab and the amazing community around it. This is just the beginning: we’ll keep doubling down on supporting its growth and innovation, while staying true to the open, collaborative spirit that made it thrive in the first place.".

Industry observers note that sentence Transformers will remain a community-driven, open-source project, with the same open-source license (Apache 2.0) as before. Contributions from researchers, developers, and enthusiasts are welcome and encouraged. The project will continue to prioritize transparency, collaboration, and broad accessibility.

The Sentence Transformers library was introduced in 2019 by Dr. Nils Reimers at the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych. Motivated by the limitations of standard BERT embeddings for sentence-level semantic tasks, Sentence-BERT used a Siamese network architecture to produce semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that could be efficiently compared using cosine similarity. Thanks to its modular, open-source design and strong empirical performance on tasks such as semantic textual similarity, clustering, and information retrieval, the library swiftly became a staple in the NLP research toolkit, spawning a range of follow-up work and real-world applications that rely on high-quality sentence representations.

In 2020, multilingual support was added to the library, extending sentence embeddings to more than 400 languages. In 2021, with contributions from Nandan Thakur and Dr. Johannes Daxenberger, the library expanded to support pair-wise sentence scoring using Cross Encoder and Sentence Transformer models. Sentence Transformers was also integrated with the Hugging Face Hub (v2.0). For over four years, the UKP Lab team maintained the library as a community-driven open-source project and provided continued research-driven innovation. During this period, the project's development was supported by grants to Prof. Gurevych by the German Research Foundation (DFG), German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and Hessen State Ministry for Higher Education, Research and the Arts (HMWK).

In late 2023, Tom Aarsen from Hugging Face took over maintainership of the library, introducing modernized training for Sentence Transformer models (v3.0), as well as improvements of Cross Encoder (v4.0) and Sparse Encoder (v5.0) models.

Industry observers note that the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, led by Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, is internationally recognized for its research in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. The lab has a long track record of pioneering work in representation learning, large language models, and information retrieval, with numerous publications at leading conferences and journals. Beyond Sentence Transformers, the UKP Lab has developed a number of widely used datasets, benchmarks, and open-source tools that support both academic research and real-world applications.

It has been revealed that hugging Face would like to thank the UKP Lab and all past and present contributors, especially Dr. Nils Reimers and Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, for their dedication to the project and for entrusting us with its maintenance and now stewardship. We also extend our gratitude to the community of researchers, developers, and practitioners who have contributed to the library's success through model contributions, bug reports, feature requests, documentation improvements, and real-world applications. We are excited to continue building on the strong foundation laid by the UKP Lab and to work with the community to further advance the capabilities of Sentence Transformers.

Setup LVM for Scalable

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that haii, pada postingan ini saya ingin sharing study case, dimana saya punya server dengan ukuran 3725.5 GB.
  • Saat pertama kali install server dalam kasus ini Ubuntu 26.04 LTS pada bagian pemartisian pilih custom dan setting agar OS tidak berjalan pada LVM.
  • Industry observers note that kita asumsikan OS sudah terinstall dan anggap kita pakai user root, langsung kita masuk ke tahap setup sisa partisi jadi lvm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that haii, pada postingan ini saya ingin sharing study case, dimana saya punya server dengan ukuran 3725.5 GB. Dengan 1 disk dan kapasitas tersebut saya memutuskan Raid0 lalu membuat LVM untuk penyimpanan data dan scalablenya, untuk tabel partisinya kira-kira seperti ini.

Saat pertama kali install server dalam kasus ini Ubuntu 26.04 LTS pada bagian pemartisian pilih custom dan setting agar OS tidak berjalan pada LVM.

Industry observers note that kita asumsikan OS sudah terinstall dan anggap kita pakai user root, langsung kita masuk ke tahap setup sisa partisi jadi lvm. Perlu diketahui server ini akan saya jalankan service docker dan mysql dimana nanti partisi /var/lib/docker dan /var/lib/mysql adalah bind mount dari LVM.

Pastikan dahulu tabel partisi dan ruang kosong.

cek dengan lsblk jika belum ke load lakukan refresh partisi.

Buat Physial Volume dari partisi yang tadi kita buat di /dev/sda4 dan verifikasi dengan pvs.

Kemudaian buat Volume Group dan verifikasi vgs.

Lalu baru kita buat Logical Volume, Jika ingin seluruh kapasitas dialokasikan untuk satu logical volume gunakan 100%FREE. Best practicenya disisakan sedikit untuk scalable biasanya 95% - 98%. Tapi pada case ini saya pakai full 100% kapasitas. Gunakan lvs untuk verifikasi.

Format partisi lvm kita agar bisa di mounting dan siap pakai, sesuai best practice kebutuhan saya memilih filesystem ext4.

Sesuai kebutuhan service saya ingin satu pool yang dipakai bersama tanpa dibagi, dan itu bisa dicapai lebih aman dengan satu LV dimount ke /mnt/data, lalu hanya Docker dan MySQL yang diarahkan ke sana.

It has been revealed that setelah itu install Docker dan MySQL seperti biasa. Keduanya otomatis menulis ke LVM lewat path default, jadi tidak perlu ubah konfigurasi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we’re excited to announce a latest collaboration between Hugging Face and VirusTotal, the world’s leading threat-intelligence and malware analysis platform. This collaboration enhances the security of files shared across the Hugging Face Hub, helping protect the machine learning community from malicious or compromised assets.

TL;DR - Starting today, every one of the 2.2M+ public model and datasets repositories on the Hugging Face Hub is being continuously scanned with VirusTotal.

It has been revealed that AI models are powerful but they’re also complex digital artifacts that can include large binary files, serialized data, and dependencies that sometimes carry hidden risks. As of today HF Hub hosts 2.2 Million Public model artifacts. As we continue to grow into the world’s largest open platform for Machine Learning models and datasets, ensuring that shared assets remain safe is essential.

By collaborating with VirusTotal, we’re adding an extra layer of protection and visibility by enabling files shared through Hugging Face to be checked against one of the largest and most trusted malware intelligence databases in the world.

In a recent development, whenever you visit a repository page or a file or directory page, the Hub will automatically retrieve VirusTotal information about the corresponding files. Example.

This provides valuable context to users and organizations before they download or integrate files from the Hub.

If you’d like to learn more about this integration or explore ways to contribute to a safer open-source AI ecosystem, reach out to security@huggingface.co.

Together, we can make AI collaboration not just open but secure by design.

I Lost Money to a 'Wrong Transfer' Scam: How to Protect Yourself and Your Team from Phishing

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, imagine you work at a shipping and customs-clearance company.
  • If you've received a message like that, you've met phishing.
  • In this guide I'll cover what phishing is, why it works even on smart people, how to protect yourself and your family first, then your company and your team, and what to do if the worst happens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, imagine you work at a shipping and customs-clearance company. An email arrives from your boss at head office asking for an urgent transfer before closing time. Or a message from a courier says your parcel is on hold until you pay a fee with your bank card, or that you've won a prize. Or a notice from a software or media service you use says your account will be closed in three hours.

If you've received a message like that, you've met phishing. It is one of the most widespread attack methods, because victims are often relaxed and act on impulse, because it costs the attacker almost nothing, and because it works often enough. I fell for one myself, and I'll tell you the story below.

In this guide I'll cover what phishing is, why it works even on smart people, how to protect yourself and your family first, then your company and your team, and what to do if the worst happens.

Phishing is pretending to be a well-known, senior, or trusted party (a bank, a coworker, a vendor, a popular platform) to trick the victim into giving up a secret or taking a harmful action: typing a password into a fake page, opening a malicious attachment, or sending money to the attacker's account.

Sources indicate that the attacker isn't breaking into your machine. They're breaking into you, through deception. That's why phishing stays effective no matter how good firewalls and antivirus get.

Attackers play on simple human feelings:.

When we're busy or tired we skim, and that's exactly the trap the attacker is betting on.

In a recent development, in 2022 I was in my office, busy preparing a major event. A WhatsApp message arrived looking like a bank notification of a transfer into my account. Then my phone rang. The caller was skilled, experienced in fraud, and spoke with complete confidence. He greeted me politely, then stated: "Sorry, we got the number wrong, money reached you by mistake." I looked at the notification, and it indicated exactly the amount he had just mentioned.

Industry observers note that it was a screenshot of an old transfer that the scammer reuses on his victims. I was talking to him on speaker while my mind was on the event, so I thanked him and, without hesitation, sent that amount from my own account and forwarded him the transfer receipt. He ended the call shortly after.

Sources indicate that then my bank's message arrived: the amount had been deducted from my balance. I opened my account on my phone and found that no extra money had come in all day. I went back to the scammer's "notification" and saw a different date and a completely different name and destination. I called him again. His phone was off, and it still is today.

Afterwards I reported it to the police, who told me they receive many reports like this. I told my staff and the trainers who work with me, then ran a training course about this kind of fraud. As for the money, I accepted the loss and moved on.

Stop before you click or transfer. Feeling rushed or scared is your cue to slow down, not to act.

Never refund money based on a receipt image. Open your bank app or statement yourself and confirm the money actually arrived. If it's real, ask the bank to return it officially.

Industry observers note that verify through a second channel. If the "bank" or "boss" writes, contact them using a number or app you already had, especially if the message came as a voice note or video, since both can be faked. Never use the contact details inside the message itself.

Recent findings suggest that turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) everywhere. It's the single most important control. Even if your password leaks, the attacker can't get in with it alone, unless you approve the prompt or hand over the code. Prefer an authenticator app or a hardware security key over SMS codes.

Industry observers note that use a password manager. A hidden security benefit: it won't autofill your password on a fake lookalike site, which is an early warning.

It has been revealed that keep everything updated. Many attacks exploit known bugs that were fixed long ago. Here's an analogy: if you keep using the same antibiotic for long stretches, it may stop working, because bacteria adapt and you have to change the drug. Systems you don't upgrade are the same: attackers learn their weaknesses and your defenses lose their effect.

Recent findings suggest that individual awareness isn't enough. We're human, and we'll slip someday. You need a guided system that becomes habit, so mistakes are less likely and less damaging.

According to recent reports, start with email, work tools, hosting consoles, and finance accounts. Use passkeys or security keys where you can: they're tied to the real domain, so they simply don't work on a fake site.

Industry observers note that these DNS records make it harder for attackers to send mail pretending to be from your domain, and they help mail providers reject forged messages. A starter DMARC record in monitoring mode looks like this:.

Read the reports, fix any legitimate senders, then move to p=quarantine and eventually p=reject.

According to recent reports, write it down: no upcoming payee, no refund, and no change to a supplier's bank details is executed without confirming against the real account statement, a phone call-back to a number already on file, and a second approver. This single rule would have stopped what happened to me, and it defeats most BEC attempts.

In a recent development, the fewer permissions an account has, the less an attacker can do with it if it's stolen. Give admin rights only to people who truly need them.

Recent findings suggest that A long yearly session is forgotten fast. Short monthly examples work better, along with simple internal phishing simulations done within legal and policy limits, to show staff what a malicious message looks like. The goal is learning, not embarrassment.

In a recent development, give people a clear button or address to report and suggest improvements about any suspicious message, and make it known that anyone who clicks the wrong link and reports it immediately is thanked, not punished. An employee who fears punishment hides mistakes, and hiding is what turns a small incident into a disaster.

Turn on your mail provider's filters and take regular backups kept separate from the main network, so a ransomware attachment doesn't mean the end of the company.

On the technical side, I built a small phishing-website detector that compares Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and SVM on the UCI Phishing Websites dataset. Random Forest reached 96.7% test accuracy. I wrote about it here: I Taught a Computer to Spot Fake Websites with 96% Accuracy. The code is open if you want to inspect or reuse it: phishing-detection-ml on GitHub. The full preprint is here.

Arabic version of this guide on Hsoub: اقرأ المقال بالعربية.

Recent findings suggest that you can't stop phishing messages from arriving, but you can make them fail. Verify through a second channel, turn on 2FA, set clear rules for money and permissions, and build a culture where everyone reports without fear. Start with one step today: turn on 2FA for your email, then share this guide with your team.

Recent findings suggest that have you faced a phishing attempt like I have? Share your story in the comments so we can all learn.

Disclosure: I drafted this article with the help of an AI assistant, and I edited and reviewed it myself. The story is my own experience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simulation has been a cornerstone in medical imaging to address the data gap. However, in healthcare robotics until now, it's often been too slow, siloed, or difficult to translate into real-world systems. That’s now changing. With new advances in GPU-accelerated simulation and digital twins, developers can design, test, and validate robotic workflows entirely in virtual environments - reducing prototyping time from months to days, improving model accuracy, and enabling safer, faster innovation before a single device reaches the operating room.

It has been revealed that that's why NVIDIA introduced Isaac for Healthcare earlier this year, a developer framework for AI healthcare robotics, that enables developers in solving these challenges via integrated data collection, training, and evaluation pipelines that work across both simulation and hardware. Specifically, the Isaac for Healthcare v0.4 release provides customers with an end-to-end SO-ARM based starter workflow and the bring your own operating room tutorial. The SO-ARM starter workflow lowers the barrier for MedTech developers to experience the full workflow from simulation to training to deployment and start building and validating autonomously on real hardware right away.

In this post, we'll walk through the starter workflow and its technical implementation details to help you build a surgical assistant robot in less time than ever imaginable before.

The SO-ARM starter workflow introduces a newly introduced way to explore surgical assistance tasks, and provides developers with a complete end-to-end pipeline for autonomous surgical assistance:.

This workflow gives developers a safe, repeatable environment to train and refine assistive skills before moving into the Operating Room.

The workflow implements a three-stage pipeline that integrates simulation and real hardware:.

Notably, over 93% of the data used for policy training was generated synthetically in simulation, underscoring the strength of simulation in bridging the robotic data gap.

The workflow combines simulation and real-world data to address the fundamental challenge that training robots in the real world is expensive and limited, while pure simulation often fails to capture real-world complexities. The approach uses approximately 70 simulation episodes for diverse scenarios and environmental variations, combined with 10-20 real-world episodes for authenticity and grounding. This mixed training creates policies that generalize beyond either domain alone.

Notably, developers could run all the simulation, training and deployment (3 computers needed for physical AI) on one DGX Spark.

With the latest LeRobot release (v0.4.0) you will be able to post-train GR00T N1.5 natively in LeRobot!

Simulation is most powerful when it's part of a loop: collect data → train → evaluate → deploy. Isaac Lab supports this full pipeline:.

This reduces time from experiment to deployment and makes sim-to-real a practical part of daily development.

Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 upgrade, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these latest multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

According to recent reports, traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

It has been revealed that similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Recent findings suggest that multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

Sources indicate that VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

In a recent development, some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

Recent findings suggest that with a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

Sources indicate that as expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

In a recent development, you might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

For retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

Sources indicate that under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The presently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

Sources indicate that the reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

In a recent development, since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

Sources indicate that the "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

It has been revealed that you may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

Sources indicate that in Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

The training companion to this post and adjacent Sentence Transformers guides:.

#195040. The Silent Override: Why Your Calibration Is Only as Good as the Layer That Owns Tone Mapping

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (655 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

The Silent Override: Why Your Calibration Is Only as Good as the Layer That Owns Tone Mapping

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A medical display can pass every calibration check and still be wrong.
  • This is the problem that separates medical display engineering from ordinary monitor QA: calibration is not a property of the panel alone; it is a property of the entire signal chain.
  • The most underdiagnosed culprit is the ICC profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A medical display can pass every calibration check and still be wrong. Not “wrong” in the sense of a dead pixel or a failed backlight—those get caught. Wrong in the sense that the grayscale curve you validated on Friday is no longer the curve the diagnostic application is actually rendering on Monday morning. No error message. No log entry. No ticket. The calibration didn’t fail. Something upstream of the display quietly took ownership of the signal.

This is the problem that separates medical display engineering from ordinary monitor QA: calibration is not a property of the panel alone; it is a property of the entire signal chain. DICOM Part 14 defines the Grayscale Standard Display Function as a target, but the target is only meaningful if every transform between the image data and the emitted luminance is accounted for—and if no unaccounted layer is allowed to override the intended baseline. In real clinical workstations, that chain includes the application, the OS color management layer, the GPU LUT, and the monitor’s internal processing. Each of these can be correct in isolation and still produce a non-conformant result when they compete.

The most underdiagnosed culprit is the ICC profile. A medical display calibrated through its internal LUT to DICOM GSDF can look perfectly conformant on a measurement report, while an OS-level ICC transform sits on top of it, remapping tone in ways the calibration never intended. The problem is not that ICC profiles are “bad.” The problem is ownership ambiguity: when both the monitor and the OS believe they are responsible for tone mapping, the effective curve becomes the composition of two transforms, neither of which was validated together. A GPU driver patch, a login event, or a display hot-plug can shift which layer wins. The clinical image changes, and nothing in the QA report reflects it.

It has been revealed that this is structurally identical to a class of bugs software engineers know well: two middlewares both “helpfully” mutating the same payload. Each is correct against its own spec. The composed system is not. In display engineering, the payload is luminance, and the mutation is invisible until someone measures the final output against a known test pattern under controlled ambient light.

The engineering response is not to pick a favorite layer and hope. It is to make the chain explicit and testable. Three practices matter more than any single product choice. First, declare a single tone-mapping owner and neutralize or deliberately manage every other transform. If the monitor’s internal calibration is the validated baseline, the OS ICC layer should not become an unmanaged second owner. Second, test at the output, not at the settings panel. A calibration report that notes “GSDF conformance achieved” is a statement about the state at calibration time, not about the state the application sees after a driver reset. End-to-end verification with an external sensor, against the actual clinical viewer, is the only test that covers composition. Third, treat driver updates and OS changes as calibration events. A GPU patch is not a neutral maintenance action in a diagnostic workstation; it can change the effective LUT behavior and silently move the display off curve.

There is a deeper lesson here that generalizes beyond radiology. The medical display problem is not a hardware problem, and it is not a “user education” problem. It is a systems integration problem with the classic shape of a silent override: a contract between layers that was never explicitly specified, never tested end-to-end, and therefore never enforced. The fix is architectural before it is clinical. If you cannot point to the layer that owns tone mapping, draw the full transform chain on a whiteboard, name every participant, and show where the final luminance is measured—then you have not validated a display. You have validated a hope. In diagnostic imaging, that hope is the only thing standing between a subtle finding and a missed one.

Tech Report: Treat the screen picker as its own step

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (332 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A recorder has two moments that look like one in a happy-path demo.
  • Industry observers note that I work on Vertov, a browser screen recorder.
  • Call getDisplayMedia() from a button press.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A recorder has two moments that look like one in a happy-path demo. The browser gives your app a screen stream, then your app starts writing a video. Give those moments separate states and test what happens in between.

Industry observers note that I work on Vertov, a browser screen recorder. Our recorder gives you a preview after you pick a source. Start recording is a separate action. That gap gives people a chance to spot the wrong tab or fix their mic before a take begins.

Call getDisplayMedia() from a button press. A browser asks the user to choose a source each time. If they close the picker, leave them at the source selection step, with their other settings intact. The same error can cover permission and policy problems, so offer a clear retry and avoid claiming you know exactly why access failed.

Recent findings suggest that open the picker, choose a scratch tab, then stop sharing from the browser before you press Record. The preview should clear and Record should become unavailable. Repeat while a short recording is running. This time the recording should finish cleanly, with its ending intact. Play the saved result to verify it. A status badge alone can’t tell you whether the final media data made it into the file.

Recent findings suggest that A screen stream may have no audio track. Browser support and the chosen capture source affect what the picker offers. Check the tracks you received and show microphone status separately from shared audio. For a useful test, record a second of tab audio with your mic off, then a second of narration with shared audio off. Play both clips back.

Industry observers note that the order I’d test is cancel, pick again, lose the source before recording, lose it during recording, then check the audio. You can try the flow in Vertov to see how a source preview and the record action work together.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • In a recent development, TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

In a recent development, TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

It has been revealed that granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

It has been revealed that phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

In a recent development, the LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

In a recent development, supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Recent findings suggest that our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

According to recent reports, we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

It has been revealed that to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

According to recent reports, after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

In this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient enhancement therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

To further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

Industry observers note that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

Industry observers note that during our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Sources indicate that figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

We also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Sources indicate that granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.
