⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
  • Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
  • It has been revealed that curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.

Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.

It has been revealed that curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.

It has been revealed that “The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik indicates. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”.

With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.

According to recent reports, the Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.

Recent findings suggest that “These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik claims. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”.

These themes, Malik says, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.

Industry observers note that through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.

Sources indicate that with Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.

The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.

Recent findings suggest that “I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.

It has been revealed that the Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.

Sources indicate that finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.

“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik says. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”.

All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik notes, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.

“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish.
  • To investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus).
  • "We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," said first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in more than 200 species of mushrooms, appears to have an unexpected effect on aggressive fish. Most mushrooms containing this compound belong to the gilled mushroom genus Psilocybe. In mammals, psilocybin interacts with serotonin receptors in the brain, influencing emotions and behaviors such as mood, appetite, and aggression. However, scientists still know relatively little about how the substance affects social interactions among animals.

To investigate this question, researchers in Canada examined the effects of psilocybin on the amphibious mangrove rivulus fish (Kryptolebias marmoratus). Their findings, published in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience, suggest that even a brief exposure to a low dose can significantly reduce aggressive behavior without disrupting normal social interactions.

"We show that an acute, low dose of psilocybin significantly reduces activity and aggressive attack behavior during social interactions in adult mangrove rivulus fish, a species that is naturally highly aggressive," said first author Dayna Forsyth, a research associate and former MSc student at Acadia University in Nova Scotia.

It has been revealed that "These findings provide the first evidence that psilocybin can selectively reduce escalated aggression in a vertebrate model without suppressing social interaction," added senior author Dr. Suzie Currie, a biologist at The University of British Columbia.

Why Scientists Studied Aggressive Mangrove Rivulus Fish.

Mangrove rivulus fish are naturally combative, particularly when they encounter another member of their species. Their aggressive responses are easy to recognize and measure, allowing researchers to detect even small changes in behavior.

These fish also have an unusual reproductive ability. They can fertilize themselves, producing offspring that are genetically identical. This makes them especially useful for experiments because scientists can minimize genetic variation and more confidently attribute behavioral differences to psilocybin rather than inherited traits.

For the experiment, the researchers worked with three genetically distinct lines of fish bred in the laboratory. One group received psilocybin, another provided the fish used to provoke social interactions, and the third helped researchers measure how much psilocybin entered and accumulated in the animals' bodies.

According to recent reports, the researchers first established a baseline for each fish's behavior. They placed a fish into a tank already occupied by another fish, with the two separated by a fiberglass mesh barrier and an opaque cover. The mesh prevented physical contact while allowing the fish to see and smell each other once the cover was removed.

After allowing five minutes for the fish to adjust to their shared environment, the team removed the opaque cover and recorded their interactions.

The following day, 24 hours after the initial observation, the researchers placed the same fish in water containing dissolved psilocybin. Following 20 minutes of exposure, they returned it to the tank with the same fish it had encountered previously. The opaque cover was then removed again so the researchers could observe any changes in behavior.

Magic Mushroom Compound Reduces Aggressive Attacks.

In a recent development, the results revealed a striking change. Fish exposed to psilocybin moved around less and displayed fewer bursts of aggressive swimming than fish that had not received the substance.

It has been revealed that to assess these changes, the scientists measured overall activity (time spent moving) and several signs of aggression (including swimming bursts). These rapid bursts are particularly important because they indicate that an encounter is escalating toward an attack, even when the fish cannot make physical contact.

According to recent reports, "Swimming bursts are high-energy attack behaviors that represent an escalation of aggression towards the stimulus fish without making physical contact," explained Currie. "Other types of aggressive behaviors, like head-on displays, are more about communication and social assessment and require very little energy.".

Interestingly, psilocybin did not suppress every form of aggressive or social behavior. While the fish became less likely to engage in intense, energy-demanding attacks, their less physically demanding social displays remained largely unchanged.

"Psilocybin's calming effect appears to selectively reduce energetically costly, escalated behaviors while lower-energy social display behaviors remained largely unchanged," said Forsyth. "This suggests that this compound can selectively dampen escalated social conflict rather than shutting down behavior altogether.".

Sources indicate that the compound also reduced general activity. When placed alongside another member of their species, fish treated with psilocybin spent less time swimming than untreated controls.

Together, these findings suggest that psilocybin may influence specific aspects of aggressive behavior rather than simply making animals less responsive to their surroundings.

What the Findings Could Mean for Psychedelic Research.

The researchers believe animal studies like this one could eventually help scientists better understand how psychedelic compounds influence behavior and identify possible directions for therapeutic research.

In a recent development, by examining which social responses are most sensitive to psilocybin, researchers may be able to uncover biological mechanisms that are difficult to investigate directly in people. Such insights could ultimately inform studies of potential clinical applications.

In a recent development, however, the team emphasized that the findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a treatment for aggression in humans. The experiment involved fish, did not evaluate any clinical intervention, and cannot establish whether similar effects would occur in people.

There are also important questions about how long the calming effect lasts. The researchers examined only single doses and short exposure periods. They did not investigate repeated treatments, long-term behavioral changes, or whether the fish might adapt to the substance over time.

Additional experiments will be necessary to determine whether psilocybin's ability to reduce aggressive attacks can persist beyond the brief period examined in this study.

"Future studies can build on this work to explore how psilocybin alters neural signaling, which serotonin pathways are involved, and why some aspects of social behavior are affected while others are not," concluded Currie. "These are questions that are difficult or impossible to answer directly in humans.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.
  • People with higher vitamin D levels tend to sleep longer and have more consistent sleep patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

People with higher vitamin D levels tend to sleep longer and have more consistent sleep patterns.

Those with higher levels also tend to spend a greater proportion of their time in bed asleep.

One proposed explanation involves melatonin, the hormone that helps signal when it is time to sleep.

The findings suggest that vitamin D status and sleep may be connected through other biological processes or shared everyday habits.

The research involved almost 80 generally healthy adults aged 18 to 45, recruited from the University of Delaware and the surrounding area.

Participants wore wrist monitors for two weeks, allowing researchers to estimate their sleep duration and timing.

Blood tests measured vitamin D levels, while urine samples provided an indicator of overnight melatonin production.

Before statistical adjustments, people whose vitamin D levels were 10 ng/mL higher slept around 12 minutes longer per night.

The association with longer sleep remained across the adjusted analyses, although several other links weakened.

Because the research was observational, it cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D improves sleep.

Sleep follows an internal rhythm that repeats roughly every 24 hours.

Light reaching the eyes helps the brain keep this rhythm aligned with the cycle of day and night.

As darkness falls, the brain normally increases its release of melatonin, helping the body prepare for sleep.

Bright artificial light late in the evening can interfere with this process and delay that signal.

Time spent outdoors and physical activity can also influence these rhythms.

Sunlight has another role in the body, allowing exposed skin to produce vitamin D.

People who spend little time outside may have more difficulty obtaining enough of the vitamin.

Food provides another source, particularly oily fish such as salmon and mackerel, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Previous research offers some evidence that vitamin D supplements may improve how people rate their sleep quality (Abboud, 2022).

A review brought together 19 intervention studies, although only three trials could be combined in its main statistical analysis.

Those trials found improvements in questionnaire scores after supplementation, but participants included people with fibromyalgia and those receiving methadone treatment.

Results for sleep duration and specific sleep disorders were less consistent, leaving questions about who might benefit and which aspects of sleep could change.

The study was published in the journal SLEEP Advances (D’Agata et al., 2025).

Industry News: 17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.
  • Recent findings suggest that we asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year.
  • (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science shows that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

Recent findings suggest that we asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

Laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together.

Josh (Upcoming Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”.

Laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories.

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature.

Angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations.

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Related GGiE practice: Superstar.

Pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a initiative, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students swiftly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Industry observers note that kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is important to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals.

It has been revealed that jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom).

Recent findings suggest that joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

Related GGiE practice: 1-2-3 Clap.

Industry observers note that david (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful.

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Related GGiE practice: Truth or Tale.

Recent findings suggest that harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices.

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”.

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back.

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness.

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions.

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a SUBSTANTIAL SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome.

Industry observers note that donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity.

Thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the upcoming school year!

We look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, what if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago?
  • Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.
  • This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago? A upcoming scientific analysis suggests that some of his ideas about the mind share surprising similarities with one of the most influential theories in modern neuroscience.

Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.

This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine. Rather than simply responding to information from the outside world, the brain is constantly anticipating what will happen next. It then compares those expectations with incoming information from the senses and works to reduce any differences between what it predicted and what actually occurred.

Scientists believe this ongoing process plays a central role in how people perceive their surroundings, make decisions, behave, and regulate emotions.

Researchers Erik Stänicke, Bendik Hovet, and Line Indrevoll Stänicke, together with colleagues, argue that this modern understanding of brain function has notable parallels with ideas that psychoanalysts have been developing for more than a century.

"For over 130 years, psychoanalysis has developed psychological theories about how predictions take place at a subjective level, which cognitive neuropsychology is now studying at a physiological level.".

How Freud's Ideas Connect to the Predictive Brain.

Although neuroscience and psychoanalysis approach the mind differently, the researchers suggest that both may be describing related processes.

Sources indicate that neuroscience examines the physical mechanisms behind thought and behavior, often using mathematical models to explain how the brain processes information. Psychoanalysis, which grew out of Freud's work, focuses more on unconscious mental processes, emotional experiences, and the ways past relationships influence present behavior.

In other words, one field investigates what happens inside the brain, while the other explores how those processes are experienced by the individual.

A particularly interesting connection involves the psychoanalytic concept of projection and the neuroscientific concept of prediction.

In psychoanalysis, projection involves attributing feelings, intentions, or qualities to someone else. The researchers suggest that this resembles how the brain uses previously learned expectations to interpret new experiences.

"When we attribute qualities, intentions or feelings to other people, our brain shapes our experience of the world in line with established expectations," claims Stänicke.

According to recent reports, for instance, someone who has repeatedly experienced rejection may become especially sensitive to signs that other people are rejecting them. Even an ambiguous remark or facial expression might be interpreted negatively because past experiences have shaped what the person expects.

Over time, these expectations can influence how someone approaches unfamiliar situations and forms latest relationships.

"This corresponds to the neuroscientific distinction between changing one's own predictions, perceptual inference, and the attempt to make the world conform to them, namely active inference.".

According to recent reports, perceptual inference refers to the way the brain interprets sensory information and updates its expectations in response. Active inference, by contrast, involves taking actions that help bring experiences into line with predictions or reduce uncertainty.

According to recent reports, together, these concepts help explain why people do not always experience the world as it objectively is. Their expectations can influence what they notice, how they interpret events, and how they respond.

Why the Brain Holds On to Negative Expectations.

The researchers believe the similarities between Freud's ideas and modern neuroscience could offer valuable insights into mental health disorders, particularly those involving deeply established patterns of thinking and behavior.

In a recent development, both approaches portray the mind as constantly seeking stability and predictability. This tendency is related to homeostasis, the process through which a system maintains a relatively stable internal state.

Recent findings suggest that in the predictive brain model, reducing uncertainty is an key part of maintaining that stability. The brain relies on familiar expectations to make the world easier to understand, even when those expectations are inaccurate or no longer helpful.

"Psychoanalysts refer to the tendency in the mind to recreate familiar relational patterns, even when these are poorly adapted," states Stänicke.

This could help explain why people sometimes repeat harmful patterns in relationships or continue interpreting situations negatively despite evidence that challenges their assumptions.

"Rigid and persistent symptoms, such as paranoid ideas or an internalized critical voice, may be stable but not very flexible prediction models," notes Stänicke.

"For example, there may be people who automatically expect criticism, rejection or hostility from others, and therefore interpret situations through this filter despite the fact that reality does not warrant it.".

According to recent reports, such expectations can become deeply entrenched because they make experiences feel familiar and predictable. Even when the resulting interpretation is distorted, maintaining an established mental model may feel less uncertain than changing it.

According to Stänicke, this offers a possible explanation for why some psychological symptoms can persist for years and why changing longstanding patterns of thought and behavior often requires considerable time.

In a recent development, the connection is particularly interesting because it suggests that some mental health difficulties may involve more than consciously held beliefs. They may also reflect deeply learned expectations that automatically shape emotional responses and interactions with others.

How Psychotherapy Could Help Change Deeply Rooted Patterns.

The researchers also highlight an important distinction between what people consciously believe and what they have learned through experience.

"In addition, both models give us insight into how parts of our expectations of the outside world are not only anchored cognitively, but in procedural memory that is expressed in relational ways of being," he says.

Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory involved in learned habits and skills. It allows people to perform familiar actions without consciously thinking through every step.

In the context of relationships, the researchers suggest that a similar form of learning may help explain why certain emotional reactions and patterns of interaction become automatic.

Someone might intellectually understand that other people are not necessarily hostile or critical, for example, yet still instinctively respond as though rejection is inevitable.

These expectations are not simply thoughts that can be changed through reasoning. They can also be embedded in habitual ways of reacting to people and navigating relationships.

This distinction may help explain why psychotherapy sometimes needs to address personal relationships and emotional experiences rather than focusing only on conscious thoughts.

Sources indicate that "Therefore, psychotherapy sometimes has to work relationally. For example, newly introduced experiences in the relationship between therapist and patient can gradually help to change entrenched relational patterns.".

Through repeated experiences that challenge familiar expectations, patients may gradually develop different ways of interpreting situations and relating to other people.

Bringing Freud's Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Together.

The researchers argue that connecting psychoanalysis with modern predictive brain theory could benefit both fields.

According to recent reports, neuroscience may provide a biological framework for understanding processes that psychoanalysts have long described through subjective experience. At the same time, psychoanalytic theories may offer more detailed explanations of how expectations are experienced emotionally, interpreted personally, and expressed through relationships.

The proposed similarities do not establish that Freud's broader theories were correct. Instead, they suggest that two very different traditions of studying the mind may offer complementary ways of understanding some of the same psychological processes.

By examining both the brain's physical mechanisms and the individual's inner experience, researchers hope to develop a more complete understanding of human behavior and mental health.

Sources indicate that "Bringing these two fields together can open up for a more holistic psychology, in which both neurological mechanisms and subjective experience are included. In this way, we can understand subjectivity in a more scientific manner.".

#194912. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.
  • Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit.
  • Sources indicate that then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love the idea of being a runner.

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

Then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Sources indicate that then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

It has been revealed that so I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

Industry observers note that I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my blueprint and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious intends produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

Success is motivating. Doing what you stated you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a significant part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate intends but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Sources indicate that missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a proposal so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

It has been revealed that across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

In short: How often beats how long.

Recent findings suggest that I hate the idea of abandoning my substantial aims. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

Break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Sources indicate that then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Sources indicate that do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

In a recent development, expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Sources indicate that every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

Recent findings suggest that at some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this upcoming behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

Sources indicate that it’s hard to abandon our grand plans and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

According to recent reports, join Christine Carter and Eli Susman on Oct. 15 for a free live conversation, with a few tiny habits to try together.

Recent findings suggest that christine Carter, Ph.D. is a Senior Fellow at the Greater Good Science Center. She is the author of The Newly introduced Adolescence: Raising Happy and Successful Teens in an Age of Anxiety and Distraction (BenBella, 2020), The Sweet Spot: How to Accomplish More by Doing Less (Ballantine Books, 2015), and Raising Happiness: 10 Simple Steps for More Joyful Kids and Happier Parents (Random House, 2010). A former director of the GGSC, she served for many years as author of its parenting blog, Raising Happiness. Find out more about Christine here.

#194910. "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2656 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

"Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered an unexpected reason why Alzheimer's disease disrupts sleep, and their findings suggest that the problem may be reversible.
  • The surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered an unexpected reason why Alzheimer's disease disrupts sleep, and their findings suggest that the problem may be reversible. In experiments involving mice with Alzheimer's-like brain changes, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day without removing the amyloid plaques associated with the disease.

The surprising discovery points to an overlooked culprit: the brain's own immune cells. Rather than simply protecting the brain from damage, these cells can trigger inflammation that interferes with healthy sleep.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at the University of Kentucky found that temporarily eliminating most of these immune cells allowed the mice to sleep longer and spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep. The results suggest a potential new approach to treating one of the most disruptive symptoms of Alzheimer's disease.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, were reported by a team led by Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., an associate professor of physiology at the University of Kentucky College of Medicine, and first author Nicholas J. Constantino, Ph.D., a recent doctoral graduate.

Macauley described the discovery as "paradigm-shifting" because it challenges the prevailing understanding of why people with Alzheimer's often experience severe sleep problems.

How the Brain's Immune System Can Disrupt Sleep.

In a recent development, to understand what the researchers uncovered, imagine a small fire breaking out in a kitchen. Instead of containing the flames, the building's sprinkler system activates everywhere, flooding the entire house and causing widespread damage.

Something similar may happen in the brain during Alzheimer's disease.

Amyloid plaques are deposits of sticky protein fragments that accumulate between nerve cells. They are one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's and have long been investigated for their role in the disease.

The brain also contains specialized immune cells known as microglia. These cells normally protect the nervous system by removing debris, responding to injuries, and helping maintain a healthy environment for neurons.

In a recent development, however, when microglia detect amyloid plaques, their defensive response can become excessive. Instead of simply addressing the threat, they release inflammatory signals that may interfere with normal brain activity.

Sources indicate that scientists have traditionally linked sleep problems in Alzheimer's primarily to damaged neurons or the accumulation of amyloid plaques. The new findings suggest that the immune system's reaction to those plaques plays a major role.

"Basically, we revealed that it is not the plaques themselves, or solely dysfunctional neurons, that cause sleep loss but actually microglia," said Macauley. "Microglia are immune cells that, when they respond to plaques, kick off this elaborate cascade of inflammation, as if the microglia are partying all night, and keeping the brain awake.".

In other words, the brain's response to Alzheimer's pathology may create additional problems beyond those caused by the plaques themselves. The researchers compared this widespread reaction to a "whole house response," in which a defense mechanism ends up causing more disruption than expected.

Tracking Alzheimer's Sleep Changes Inside the Brain.

Industry observers note that to investigate the connection between microglia and sleep, the scientists studied two groups of mice. One group was genetically predisposed to develop amyloid plaques, while the other consisted of normal "wild-type" mice that experienced typical aging.

The researchers examined the animals at two ages: six months, when plaques first appeared in the genetically modified mice, and 18 months, when the disease model indicated more advanced pathology.

Comparing these groups helped the scientists distinguish changes associated with Alzheimer's pathology from those that naturally occur as the brain ages.

The team used several advanced technologies to measure sleep and examine what was happening inside the brain.

Each mouse was fitted with a small device that recorded electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG).

In a recent development, EEG measures the brain's electrical activity, including the patterns and rhythms produced when networks of neurons communicate. These electrical signals change depending on whether the brain is awake, dreaming or experiencing deep sleep.

EMG measures electrical activity in muscles. Combining the two techniques allowed researchers to identify different sleep stages and determine how long the animals remained in each one.

The scientists also wanted to visualize the relationship between amyloid plaques and immune cells throughout the brain.

For this, they used light-sheet microscopy, an imaging technique that makes biological tissue transparent and illuminates it with a thin layer of laser light. The resulting images can be assembled into detailed three-dimensional maps, allowing scientists to examine structures that would otherwise be difficult to see.

This approach revealed the distribution of plaques and microglia across the brain, helping researchers understand where immune cells were responding to Alzheimer's pathology.

Scientists Temporarily Remove 87% of Brain Immune Cells.

To determine whether microglia were actually responsible for disrupted sleep, the team conducted an experiment designed to temporarily eliminate most of these cells.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers administered a drug called Pexidartinib (PLX3397), which was originally developed for cancer research. It blocks a cellular signal that microglia depend on for survival.

After the mice received the medication in their food for 14 days, approximately 87% of their microglia had been depleted.

This allowed the scientists to test whether sleep would improve when the cells driving the inflammatory response were largely absent.

The researchers also performed a detailed analysis of the animals' brain activity using a mathematical method called Fitting Oscillations and One Over Frequency (FOOOF).

This technique separates electrical signals into periodic activity (the rhythmic waves we usually think of as brain waves) and aperiodic activity (the background electrical noise).

By examining these different components, the team could identify changes in how the brain was functioning, including whether it remained unusually active during periods when it should have been resting.

The process is somewhat like monitoring a car engine to determine whether it continues running at high speed even when the vehicle is supposed to be idle.

A Surprising Discovery About Alzheimer's Brain Plaques.

Macauley called the results "mind-blowing and unexpected.".

One of the most surprising findings was that sleep problems did not continue worsening as amyloid plaques accumulated.

In a recent development, the researchers initially expected that increasing plaque buildup would lead to progressively more severe sleep disturbances. Instead, the mice developed substantial sleep problems relatively early, and those problems remained largely unchanged even as plaque levels increased dramatically.

According to recent reports, "I expected that as plaque burden became more severe, sleep disruption would also worsen," noted Constantino. "The disruptions in sleep and cortical EEG activity that occur at 6 months, when plaques first emerge, did not worsen by 18 months, despite more than double the amount of plaque burden.".

The team described this pattern as a ceiling effect. Essentially, sleep disruption appeared to reach a certain level early in the disease process rather than increasing in direct proportion to the amount of amyloid in the brain.

Recent findings suggest that this suggests that the initial inflammatory response triggered by plaques may be particularly important. Once microglia become activated and disrupt sleep, additional plaque accumulation may not necessarily produce an equivalent increase in sleep loss.

The discovery offers an vital clue as to why sleep disturbances can emerge relatively early in Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Disrupts a Different Type of Sleep Than Normal Aging.

The study also revealed a notable difference between sleep changes caused by normal aging and those associated with Alzheimer's pathology.

Industry observers note that sleep is not a single, uniform state. Throughout the night, the brain moves through several stages that perform different functions.

Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is strongly associated with vivid dreaming and plays an important role in processing memories. The researchers found that normal aging primarily reduced this type of sleep.

In a recent development, alzheimer's pathology, however, had a different effect. It selectively disrupted non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, which includes the deepest and most physically restorative stages of sleep.

In a recent development, during NREM sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions that support learning, memory, and recovery. Deep sleep is also associated with processes that help clear metabolic waste products from the brain.

"That restorative sleep is super important for physical repair, learning and memory and washing out the toxins of the day," Macauley remarked.

Losing this important stage of sleep could have consequences beyond daytime fatigue.

Because healthy sleep helps maintain the brain's internal environment, disruptions may interfere with processes that normally remove potentially harmful waste. Researchers suspect this could contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle in which Alzheimer's pathology disturbs sleep, and inadequate sleep may further aggravate the disease.

Breaking that cycle could therefore become an notable treatment strategy.

More Than Two Hours of Sleep Restored Without Removing Plaques.

The most striking result emerged after the researchers temporarily removed most of the microglia from the brains of mice with Alzheimer's-like pathology.

The animals gained more than two hours of sleep per day.

They also experienced longer periods of restorative NREM sleep, giving them more opportunities to transition naturally into REM sleep, which is important for memory formation.

Even more surprisingly, these improvements occurred without any reduction in amyloid plaque levels.

The plaques were still present, but the mice were sleeping substantially better.

This finding provides evidence that the inflammatory response driven by microglia contributes directly to sleep disruption and that suppressing this response can reverse at least some of the associated sleep problems.

It also suggests that researchers may not need to eliminate amyloid plaques to improve sleep in Alzheimer's disease.

Although these findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and the same benefits have not yet been demonstrated in people. Temporarily removing most of the brain's immune cells is also not an established or practical treatment for Alzheimer's patients.

The researchers are now interested in whether the beneficial effects can be reproduced by adjusting microglial activity rather than eliminating the cells themselves.

If such an approach eventually proves successful in humans, it could provide a way to improve sleep and potentially reduce some of the additional stress that poor sleep places on the brain.

The Research Team Behind the Discovery.

The work was conducted in Macauley's laboratory in the Department of Physiology at the University of Kentucky's Sanders-Brown Center on Aging.

Macauley credits the achievement to a "beautiful partnership" with students and researchers who were willing to challenge established ideas about Alzheimer's disease.

"I love people who take initiative, find their passion, are curious, and keep pushing to find an answer," Macauley noted.

She encourages members of her laboratory to be "calculated risk-takers," emphasizing that meaningful discoveries often require scientists to investigate possibilities that may initially seem unlikely.

A quote from hockey legend Wayne Gretzky hangs in her office: "You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.".

Constantino, who recently completed his doctorate at the university, remarked the laboratory's collaborative environment encouraged him to pursue questions that crossed traditional scientific disciplines.

In a recent development, "Dr. Macauley has also taught me to embrace uncertainty and failure as part of the scientific process," Constantino noted. "Some of the most interesting studies I have been a part of emerged because our original hypothesis was wrong.".

Macauley reinforces this mindset with a simple instruction to her team: "Follow the data, ask better questions, and figure out what is actually happening.".

That approach helped the researchers move beyond the traditional emphasis on neurons and amyloid plaques to examine the broader role of the brain's immune system.

Could Existing Medications Help Restore Sleep in Alzheimer's?

The research team is now exploring ways to translate these findings into treatments and diagnostic tools that could eventually benefit people with Alzheimer's disease.

One promising direction involves calming overactive microglia without removing them.

Industry observers note that because microglia perform essential protective functions, eliminating them is not an ideal long-term strategy. Instead, the researchers hope to modify how these immune cells respond to amyloid plaques and regulate inflammation.

The laboratory is investigating existing medications, including the diabetes drug Metformin and the anti-seizure medication Stiripentol.

According to recent reports, these drugs are being studied for their potential to alter how microglia produce and use energy, a process known as cellular metabolism. Changing that energy use could potentially reduce excessive immune activation and its harmful effects on sleep.

The hope is to prevent the brain's inflammatory response from becoming so intense that it disrupts normal sleep activity.

Researchers are particularly interested in whether intervention during the earlier stages of Alzheimer's could improve sleep and quality of life before substantial memory loss develops.

"If we can target that process, it might help with quality of life, attention, cognition and confusion," Macauley remarked.

The proposed drug strategies remain experimental for this purpose, and additional research will be necessary to determine whether they can safely produce similar benefits in humans.

A Simpler Way to Detect Early Alzheimer's Changes.

Beyond identifying a potential treatment target, the study uncovered electrical activity patterns that may help distinguish Alzheimer's pathology from normal brain aging.

The researchers believe these patterns could eventually make EEG a useful tool for detecting and monitoring changes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Unlike more expensive imaging procedures, EEG records electrical signals through electrodes placed on the scalp. It is relatively affordable, does not require surgery, and can be repeated to follow changes over time.

The team envisions EEG becoming a "readily accessible, affordable and longitudinal biomarker of Alzheimer's disease.".

A biomarker is a measurable biological sign that provides information about a person's health or a particular disease. A longitudinal biomarker can be tracked repeatedly to monitor how a condition develops or changes.

"Portable EEG systems could allow us to monitor people in their home environments and potentially screen for changes associated with an Alzheimer's disease, without the initial need for expensive or invasive tests," Macauley stated.

If future human studies confirm the usefulness of these electrical signatures, portable EEG devices might eventually help doctors identify people who need additional testing.

This could be particularly valuable in rural communities across Kentucky, where patients sometimes must travel long distances to reach specialized medical centers.

Instead of requiring every potentially at-risk patient to undergo advanced testing immediately, local clinics might use simpler monitoring tools to identify individuals who would benefit from further evaluation.

Although this application still requires validation, it offers a possible path toward more accessible Alzheimer's screening and monitoring.

Ultimately, the study suggests that treating Alzheimer's may require looking beyond the plaques themselves and examining how the brain responds to them.

By identifying the immune cells responsible for much of the sleep disruption in their mouse models, the University of Kentucky researchers have uncovered a potential way to restore an essential brain function without first removing the underlying amyloid deposits.

The next challenge is determining whether calming these cells can deliver similar benefits in people, potentially improving sleep, cognition and quality of life long before the most severe symptoms of Alzheimer's develop.

Seven Ways to Outlast Political Authoritarianism
